speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That a select committee to be designated be appointed to consider with Mr. Speaker the procedure of this house for the purpose of suggesting any changes that may be desirable to assure the more expeditious dispatch of public business, with power to send for persons and papers, and to report from time to time its findings and recommendations to the house.
He said: Mr. Speaker, hon. members will recall that there was a committee on procedure established during the last session of parliament which held meetings up to very near the end of the session, and which brought in a report recommending that a committee be set up again at this session, at an early date. The purpose of this motion is to ask the house to act in conformity with the recommendation contained in that report.
I think it is recognized by all members of the house that an effort should be made to bring about a more orderly manner of handling the business of the house, and that it should be possible to do that without in any way curbing unduly or limiting unduly the freedom of speech and discussion in matters concerning the country's business.
There have been various ways suggested. One of the minor ways was an improvement in the manner of handling resolutions respecting the introduction of bills with monetary applications; and I think we were all very pleased the other day when it was possible to deal with the formalities of fifteen resolutions in a matter of only two or three minutes, instead of fifteen times that amount of time which would have been required had those formalities been carried out in the usual fashion.
I do not think anyone would seek the elimination of the traditional formalities that have their place in the proper handling of the business of the house; but I think hon. members in all parts of the house would wish to have that done in a manner which would leave as much time as possible for the consideration of the less formal aspects of the business of the house.
I understand it is by general agreement that this motion is placed before Your Honour today and that, though there are varying views as to the advisability of some of the amendments to the rules that were considered last year, there is the general feeling that an attempt should be made to improve those rules and that the matter should be disposed of as expeditiously as the proper consideration of it will permit.
I do not think I can add anything more because the terms of the resolution in themselves appear to be terms that should commend themselves to the judgment of the house: "for the purpose of suggesting any changes that may be desirable to assure the more expeditious dispatch of public business."
I think that is the goal each and every one of us would have in mind-but only such changes as "may be desirable." I believe we would agree that it is not desirable to have rules that permit of obstruction, but neither is it desirable to have rules that interfere with the proper exercise of the responsibilities of each of us to discuss those matters that are properly before the house.
I would hope that the committee could be set up at an early date and that it would, as I am sure it will, envisage its responsibilities in the light of the dignity of parliament and the great price we all attach to free democratic processes in dealing with public affairs.

Mr. Speaker, I have no doubt the present resolution will receive the unanimous support of the house. May I express my own pleasure at seeing the motion brought on early, because I think it is helpful that this committee should be set up at an early date.
The terms of reference are identical with those that have been approved by the house now on three previous occasions. Actually the committee is now in the course of being appointed for the fourth consecutive session. That is not to say that the committee has been dilatory in its work in the past; I do not think that can be fairly said. But the task is not an easy one, and the committee has, I think, taken a fairly comprehensive view of its responsibilities. With the proposal that effort be made to expedite the transaction of public business in this house, I am sure there will be agreement. Certainly,

Special Committee on Procedure those who sit in this part of the house will give every co-operation to any sound method for transacting the business of Canada in this place in a proper and expeditious manner, provided that it is done in keeping with the essential rights of members of this house, all of them, and with due regard for the dignity and decorum which ought to characterize the transaction of the business of this country.
May I say also that I am glad to see on the order paper, in response to suggestions that have come from us in this part of the house in the past, and notably from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), a greater volume of government business than has appeared on the order paper at this stage in past sessions. I think that is an indication of desire on the part of the government to help all in this house to contribute on their part to expediting the business of the house.
Now, sir, there is one matter that does not require more than casual mention. When this committee was set up two years ago, in January, 1953, I raised the point that occasion might arise for widening somewhat the terms of reference. The Prime Minister at that time said that if any such occasion arose he would see to it that the matter was brought before the house and every assistance given to the committee in making sure its terms of reference were wide enough to do whatever it thought necessary in the way of review of the rules. Actually, in the discussion in the committee, it has not yet been found necessary to ask the house for any widening of terms; but I presume if such a situation should arise the Prime Minister would be good enough to indicate that co-operation will be given in bringing that matter before the house as soon as possible.
Sir, I do not know whether, when the committee makes its report-and I have no doubt it will make its final report at this session-it will be possible for the house to receive the report with the same unanimity that has characterized the proceedings of the house today; but certainly as to the setting up of this committee I am sure there will be general agreement in the house.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we too welcome the proposal that this committee on procedure be established at an early date, and we shall be glad to place our members on the committee and give the question of house business our very serious consideration. However, I feel that once again I must make the point which we feel very strongly, namely, that the rules of the house are the possession of the whole house. They are the
[Mr. Fleming.!

rules of parliament across the years, not the rules of any one session of parliament, or of any parliament between two elections. 1 realize the problem that that creates, because we are in a democracy in which the majority governs. But I suggest that with respect to the rules of parliament particular care has to be taken that a government majority does not use that majority to make rules which unduly, if I may use the Prime Minister's words, interfere with the freedom of speech and the rights of all of us who are here.
I remind hon. members that it is a long time, 28 years, I believe, since the last general revision of the rules of this house was made. That means that the members of parliament in 1927 were making rules not just for themselves but for a good many parliaments that have followed. We shall have to take that approach in this committee, and I urge very strongly that it be recognized right from the start, not that unanimity must be required for any change, but that there be pretty general agreement amongst the representatives of both sides of the house, amongst representatives of all parties, before any very serious changes are made.
Just to make it crystal clear, Mr. Speaker, that I do not mean by that that I am opposed to any changes that interfere with any of our existing practices, I want to repeat what I have already said in public and in this session, that I think we can well afford, on a fair basis to everybody, without unduly interfering with the rights of free speech, to cut the 40-minute limit on speeches down to 30 minutes. There is objection to that from some quarters, I have no doubt, but 1 want to make it clear that in asking for general agreement to be the basis of any change, it is not simply a case of my objecting to any and all changes, because there is this change I have suggested to which I am prepared to agree, and there are others as well.
It seems to me the principle should be, is the change fair to all members of the house, or is it a change that interferes with the rights of any particular section of the house? We have to be particularly careful that the majority does not use its power to interfere with the rights of the minority. In that vein I mention in particular the long-established traditional rights that belong to all private members respecting the raising of grievances and the discussing of expenditures of public moneys. I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that when it comes to any changes affecting the right to raise grievances on going into supply, when it comes to limiting

discussion of expenditure of public funds, I think those on the committee from the other side know that they will find in us on this side a certain degree of obstinacy.
We feel that these traditional rights should be protected very carefully, and the responsibility for that protection rests just as much on those who constitute the majority in this house as it does on those of us who are in the minority. I say again I am glad to have this committee established, and I am glad it is being established early. We shall give the work of that committee our best and most serious attention in the hope that some changes in the rules that will help to expedite the business of the house can be made at this session. But let us remember that, through all of this, what we are dealing with is not the rules for one session or for one parliament. They are the rules of parliament as a whole across the years.

I might say that we in this group are also glad that this motion to set up a committee on procedure has been brought on in the early days of the session. We believe it is possible to take steps to expedite the business and efficiency of the house without seriously impairing the privileges and the rights of the members, and we certainly believe that it would be of importance to cut the length of speeches from 40 minutes to 30 minutes. We believe that by so doing we would be improving the speeches because so often a lot of padding is put in a speech in order to fill out the 40 minutes.
We trust that it will be possible at this session for this committee to make greater progress than it has been able to do in the past.

Mr. Speaker, as has been said, I do not wish unduly to delay the passing of this resolution, but I have the conviction that we shall have considerable discussion in this house if any report is brought back from the committee, and perhaps it would be better to have a little of that discussion before we go into committee so that we shall have some idea of where we stand. I have to say that I have noticed recently a feeling that the time of parliament in session should be cut down. That seems strange after the action we took last year to see that we were fairly well remunerated for the time we were here. I have seen throughout the press during the recess expressions of opinion in regard to parliament that did neither credit to the institution of parliament itself nor to the newspapers but was apt, in my opinion, to raise doubts in the minds of people as regards parliament's value. Now perhaps we could shorten the
Special Committee on Procedure time we are here by hurrying up the procedure and by rushing things through. I believe that in the Soviet union they get away with one-day sessions. Possibly those who are impatient of the time the members hold up the house would not go that far, but that is a target that we could have in mind.
Let me draw to the attention of the house the purpose for which the rules as they are have been made, as expressed by one Hatsell who dealt with precedents on proceedings in the House of Commons quite a while ago in 1818. We find that citation 900, in Beau-chesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, second edition, states:
So far the maxim is certainly true and founded on good sense that as it is always in the power of the majority by their numbers to stop any improper measures proposed on the part of their opponents, the only weapon by which the minority can defend themselves from similar attempts from those in power are the forms and rules and proceedings which have been found necessary from time to time and are become the standing orders of the house, by a strict adherence to which the weaker party can alone be protected from those irregularities and abuses which these forms were intended to check, and which the wantonness of power is but too often apt to suggest to large and successful majorities.
I hope the large and successful majorities in this house will restrain themselves somewhat and in their own interests be sure that the minority has all the time and all the opportunity which is available to them to express themselves in this house.
I have served on most of the committees on procedure that have been set up since I came here, with the exception of one session when through illness I was not able to serve, and I hope I can be on the committee this year when it is set up. I am sure we can come to some understanding as to the recommendations to be made to this house to better streamline the procedure, provided of course that the government members are not too impatient with those of us who are anxious to maintain those privileges which we have.
I remember when serving on the committee last year that the leader of the house asked the opposition members, and perhaps he asked all of the members, at the conclusion of the committee's deliberations, if they had any further suggestions to make as to how the rules could be improved. I recall telling him that I was not going to make any suggestions as to how my own abilities, if that is the proper word to use, to criticize the government might be curtailed, but I told him that I was willing if we got something in exchange.

Joint Committee on Criminal Law
I heard over the radio last Sunday night a comment attributed to Sir John A. Macdonald concerning horse-trading. If I might paraphrase this I would say I think we will stand solidly on fundamentals but we will horse-trade on details.

As a relatively young man in terms of service as far as this house is concerned, I am a little reluctant to offer advice but I certainly welcome the proposed setting up of this committee because I believe very deeply in this matter-that the great strength of our system of parliament is due to the fact that it is made up of a great cross-section of all types of people in this country.
There are some of us who are not professional politicians and there are some of us who do not want to sit here all the time, nor should this become a place for those who have already made their mark in the business field and are looking for what little bit of honour may be attached to this place. I think that we can keep our system strong only if this house continues to attract to it a broad cross-section of people in this country.
I just wanted to say that at this time, and I am looking forward to some tangible results from this committee.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture. subtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT OF ACT TO COVER FLOODED ACREAGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to express my appreciation to the hon. member for having given me notice of his question. I would like to read to the house the section of the act which would have to be amended if the suggested action were undertaken:
(d) "cultivated land" means land that in the year of award was seeded to crop or in summer fallow and includes land seeded to grass in any year if the productivity thereof was maintained in the year of award;
With regard to the phrase in the question "intended to be seeded", I do not know of any way in which we can amend the act in order to make it possible to have a provision of that kind. If we were going to amend the act it would have to take under consideration the fact that what is being pressed upon us at this time is something entirely different from anything we had in mind when the act was passed. The act was passed to take care of drought and the terms of it are sufficiently loose that we have been able to apply it to flooded areas under certain circumstances.
There is some question as to the manner in which it would be amended if it were decided to do so and it is of course a matter which will be given consideration. But I would like to point out that that was not the intention of the act when placed on the statute book.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) and his parliamentary assistant, perhaps I might be permitted to answer on behalf of

The Address-Mr. Masse the minister the question asked yesterday by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) which reads as follows:
Can the minister give the house any information about the sale of Canadian National hotels, with particular reference to the safeguarding of the rights of the employees concerned?
The management of the Canadian National Railways advise that they have accepted an offer from a Canadian syndicate headed by Mr. Walter F. Thorn, of Moose Jaw, Saskatchewan, to purchase the Prince Arthur hotel, Port Arthur; the Prince Edward hotel, Brandon; and two summer resorts, Minaki lodge and Pictou lodge.
Some months ago an unsolicited offer was received by the railway, and subsequently the management published a series of advertisements inviting interested parties, particularly local community interests, to submit other offers.
Only one all-inclusive offer was made, which was from the individual originally interested.
Before the properties are transferred as going concerns, which will be March 1, officials of the Canadian National Railways will visit Port Arthur and Brandon to interview the staffs of the hotels.
The two resort hotels are, of course, serviced almost entirely by temporary employees.
The management advise it is the policy of the new owners to maintain the hotels' traditional high standard of service and efficiency. The syndicate have stated that in line with this policy a program of capital expenditures has been planned for all four hotels to begin early in 1955.
With regard to the second part of the hon. member's question, the management advise that those employees eligible to exercise their seniority rights in accordance with the wage agreements will be able to transfer to other Canadian National hotels if they wish to do so.
I might add that the management are making a press announcement today substantially along the above lines.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday when dealing with agricultural matters in my constituency, I said it was urgent that the government maintain the support of farm prices, especially as far as butter is concerned, as it is one of the main sources of income for the majority of our Quebec farmers.
I also stated that because lumbering and farming are the two sources of adequate income, it is urgent and necessary that they receive the same attention from our governments.
I also mentioned that 75 per cent of my constituency is made up of wooded lots, three-quarters of which are but some 50 years old and that during the past 10 years privately-owned timber limits have been worked beyond their possibilities.
I would like to say something to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) about his appreciation of the province of Quebec, my province. I listened closely to some of the things he had to say, and I read the whole of his unbecoming statement on the residents of my province. I believe I am warranted in saying that I know that province from east to west and from north to south, having travelled through it on several occasions in the course of my professional duties. When the hon. member asserts that it is ripe for communism, it is a pleasure for me to take it up and say, as an answer, that as long as no socialist party succeeds in taking root in Quebec, communism is not to be feared. I am also under the impression

that the information made available to him came from certain groups of unsuccessful socialists who carry no weight with the authorities of my province.
Moreover, with respect to his statement in which he mentioned his meeting with two Catholic priests, I would advise him, if opportunity offers again, to go to the ecclesiastical authorities and ask them what they think of the people under their jurisdiction.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: He gave no names though.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The province of Quebec, like every other province, for that matter, has contributed to the development and expansion of this nation of ours. When one is aware of the spirit of tradition in the parishes of Quebec province, where the land has been cleared by families established there for three hundred years and who have been there ever since, settled on the property of their ancestors, it is not difficult to understand the feelings of my fellow citizens. When we really understand how these people are attached to their family and their parish and how good their relations are with the established authority, we need have no fear of communism there.
I am by no means happy to have to make remarks such as these which may seem to be a reflection upon another hon. member, but I feel it is my duty to protest and to defend the honour of my constituents.
I am not particularly surprised by some remarks coming from members on the opposite side, who would have us believe that everything is wrong with the administration of this country. Those are the same complaints that we hear every year. I want these members to know that I am a Liberal by principle, that I believe the Liberal party has done more than any other for the development of Canada in the past fifty years. It was the Liberal party, headed by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, which contributed most to the expansion of Canada, through the establishment of the transcontinental railway and through its efforts to unite provinces having different mental habits and speaking different languages. It was another Liberal leader, the Righ Hon. Mackenzie King, who for the first time concerned himself with the welfare of big families by the adoption of family allowances and of the first legislation to better the condition of labour. And, in these days, it is not a mere result of circumstances if our Canadian economy is undergoing such extensive development. It is due to the foresight of the present Prime Minister. I am convinced that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) is entitled to his share of credit for the rapid expansion of
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker our natural resources in general. It is because this party's membership includes men who, looking to the future, have succeeded in convincing the most brilliant graduates of our universities to contribute to the development of Canada.
With a Liberal government such as we have -today, the youth of my province -and of the whole of my country can look forward to the future with confidence, provided they properly fertilize the furrows so finely traced for them.

Mr. Speaker, I am one of those who believe that a manner of saving the time of the house would be to discontinue the repetition of the congratulations that are invariably extended to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I think those congratulations may be taken for granted after they have been extended by the leaders of the respective parties.
I am going to deal with a number of matters this afternoon that I believe are of interest to the people of Canada as a whole. However, before doing so, may I say this is the first opportunity I have had to deal with a situation that I have brought before parliament on previous occasions, namely, the pollution of the North Saskatchewan river and the need of immediate action being taken to meet the situation that again prevails on that river this year. Within the last few days pollution has again attacked the water supply of the cities of Prince Albert and North Battleford. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) have been communicated with and, without going into detail on this occasion, I believe that the time has come, and is long overdue, when action should be taken with regard to the question of interprovincial rivers to the end that pollution of these rivers by industry or -by any body or individual whatsoever shall not be permitted.
Last session I endeavoured on a number of occasions to secure an amendment to the Criminal Code making it an offence punishable with serious penalties to allow pollution to take place at any place where the water supply of any town or city is interfered with. I again repeat that suggestion. Indeed, I understand that the mayor of Prince Albert, Mr. David Stuart, has appealed within the last two or three days on behalf of the city council of the city of Prince Albert for assistance and has asked for effective action to permit of the control of interprovincial streams, particularly such streams as are used as a source of a domestic water supply.

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker
The situation is a serious one for those cities. The council of Prince Albert at a meeting held a day or so ago placed the responsibility upon the federal government, and I believe that one of the major ways in which that responsibility can be discharged is by placing a section in the Criminal Code to cover the offence. I would like to see set up an interprovincial board on water pollution, a board similar to the board of transport commissioners, which would have power to recommend what is necessary to preserve interprovincial waters for the Canadian people, rather than permit them to be detrimentally affected by the wrongful action of individuals or corporations in another province.
The speech from the throne is an interesting document. The government is a changed one. I doubt whether in your experience in this house, Mr. Speaker, you have ever seen a more subdued government, as they face up to conditions that prevail in this country. The Prime Minister spoke with urbanity and a brilliant lack of promises of action regarding these problems. Mr. King said on occasion that speeches from the throne were to conceal rather than to reveal. On that basis this is indeed a masterpiece.
I must mention another question while the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is in the house. A few minutes ago the long expected answer to the attempted resignation by Mr. Thomson was given. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) says in effect that the resignation was not to be effective until November 30, or in other words until after the Liberal convention in the province of Saskatchewan had taken place and when it was over it was found necessary to keep him in the public service, because there was no one else who could fill the position of director of P.F.R.A. Mr. Speaker, can you imagine what a catastrophe would have occurred had he been chosen as Liberal leader in the province of Saskatchewan!
Playing ball with a position in any department of government in that manner is not conducive to keeping organizations headed by such a person, however eminent he may be, from being touched by the suggestion of political partisanship. I believe everyone in the public service-and I have taken this stand on previous occasions-may remove himself from the public service if he desires to take public office.
But does that justify a resignation that simply is postponed until the outcome of an uncertain event? I think one of the reasons for the success of the convention-and it was a successful convention, based upon


numbers present-was the fact that there was free discussion. People tell me that the reason for the success of the convention measured by numbers present was the fact that Simmie and "Jimmie" and "Gimrnie" Thomson were engaged in controversy before the convention: "Give me the leadership or give me my job back."
What did Mr. Simmie say? Are there politics in P.F.R.A.? Many persons in the organization are doing their best, and resent what has taken place in this case. What did Mr. Simmie say regarding P.F.R.A. and, in general, the attempt on the part of Mr. Thomson to play ball with a position of responsibility in the service of the crown? He said this:
It seems I did not make myself clear. I believe that Mr. Gardiner is in control of a political machine, and that he is using or causing P.F.R.A. and P.F.A.A. to be used for political purposes, and that constitutes unwarranted interference with the leadership race.
And on another occasion, setting out his views of the situation, he said this:
I am saying there is something wrong in Saskatchewan. I say it with all my heart, that Mr. Gardiner does not know what is going on. The P.F.R.A. and the P.F.A.A. are being used as a political arm for somebody. I am saying that if Mr. Gardiner knew it he would not allow it.
Mr. Speaker, this type of thing is detrimental to the preservation of a non-political civil service. It is the kind of thing which endangers the inviolability of the civil service. There is no justification for a government's receiving a resignation which is dependent for its determination upon a contingent result, and then restoring that person to his position in the civil service after he has participated in a political manner and for political purposes during the interval before his resignation is considered.
The speech from the throne reveals but little. The Prime Minister is about to leave for Great Britain, there to represent Canada. While in England he is to receive the honour of the freedom of the city of London. What is he going to do when he is over there? What stand does he intend to take before that conference of commonwealth prime ministers? How will he speak for Canada? That we do not know. Of that we have no knowledge. We do know one thing, that if anybody suggests to him that he or his government has done anything to separate the links between Canada and the commonwealth, he will be able to answer.
You will remember that in 1949 appeals to the privy council were abolished, except for actions then in the course of being proceeded with in the courts. Do you remember the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) as he clothed his words in lachrymose tones describing the

appeal to the privy council as this "badge of colonialism", and contending that it "was unworthy of the sacrifices and the efforts of our fellow Canadians, and undeserving of the bounty which Providence has bestowed upon our country" to have appeals to the privy council. In other words, to appeal from the Supreme Court of Canada was to undermine the sacred prestige of that body.
In the last few weeks this government, dissatisfied with the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada on a tax case, is taking one of the last of the appeals to the privy council. The Prime Minister when he goes to the United Kingdom will be able to say that there is one link the government is going to maintain to the last-and that is the right to use the facilities of appeal in any case of a decision in our own court, with all its prestige, with all its power, and all its ability, with which the government disagrees.
Mr. Speaker, what manner of consistency is this?
In the last ten days, three of the senior ministers went to Washington, namely, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), to do what they should have been doing for the last several years, protesting against the gutting of GATT by the United States, the policy of the United States in recent years in interfering with our right to export farm products into that country. That right should not have been interfered with. Are we not all together endeavouring to achieve freedom? Does the United States not require our great mineral resources for the preservation of the legions of freedom? What happened on that trip? We do not know, Mr. Speaker. Their trip was just as revealing as the speech from the throne. But there is one thing that annoyed Canadians when they read of it in the press and that was that when those ministers arrived there was nobody from the United States state department at the airport to welcome them. It came over the radio that they had been snubbed. Canadians resented that. The next day it was cleared up by a Canadian spokesman in the state department who said: "Not snubbed, just forgotten". Placing quotas and embargoes should not be expected at any time, much less at this time, having regard to the international problems which we face together.
I am not going to traverse ground that has already been covered. I am going to deal first with the C.C.F. subamendment. This is the first time that the C.C.F. has come out from under the bam and revealed that it
The Address

Mr. Diefenbaker intends to have planners to plan for Canada the way they planned for Saskatchewan. I can tell you this, as far as Saskatchewan is concerned-

speechtext: No Tory party.

speechtext:
The planners have been bunglers in practically everything they have undertaken in connection with industrial development. I believe in private enterprise. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said the other day that he believed in it. I was a little surprised at that because after all the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Pickersgill), who in some ways has become political mentor to the senior members of the government, made a speech only recently, and it is reported on November 6, when he said:
The phrase "private enterprise" was a "Tory trademark" and Liberals should never use it.
I would like to hear what the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) will say to the political philosopher when he reads that ejaculation. Then he goes on to say:
The trademark of the party I belong to is "human welfare", and without working for this we do not deserve the power of office.
Having regard to some of the legislation setting up these national government crown corporations or state monopolies, one may wonder whether the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration does not in truth represent the viewpoint of the government. Mr. Speaker, over the years the C.C.F. has been producing a rolled-up subamendment with everything in it-socialism hidden in one of the subsections-and when you voted against it they said you were voting against something in that subamendment that you should have been in favour of. That is all over now.
In the subamendment hon. members are asked to vote for the adoption of socialism, to vote for the planners. The theories of the planners of 1944 in the province of Saskatchewan have been dissipated in the light of experience. They promised social security without anybody paying for it. They promised to set up corporations because business means profit. They went into industry after industry. The wreckage of their abortive venture is strewn over Saskatchewan, as examples: a shoe factory, a tannery, a woollen mill. These things blossomed, Mr. Speaker, and then withered, and the leading planners, too.
They were costly ventures. A box factory in Prince Albert is still operating. Men have been put out of work, laid off in recent months and advised that if they raise any objection the factory will be closed. There is a labour act in effect in Saskatchewan that

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker demands arbitration. The government has refused arbitration to employees of government corporations. The plans of the planners have been dissipated in the solid school of experience.

speechtext: How many Tories have you elected in Saskatchewan since 1933?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My hon. friend interrupts, but his interruption has no reference to what I am dealing with. Will he say that the myth which is essential to the socialist philosophy, the superiority of government over private enterprise, has been proven or established in Saskatchewan? Venture capital has been kept out. The planners used to say that the state would take over the natural resources. They planned, and when Saskatchewan found itself at the end of the western parade in development the premier of the province laid out the red carpet for the great capitalists of New York.
They are always contending that they indeed are the custodians of the privileges of labour. What have they done in Saskatchewan? Some of the employees of the crown corporations in Saskatchewan asked for wage increases and were refused. Mr. Douglas said that "under present conditions no group of the community is entitled to a larger share of a smaller cake". Where is the philosophy of 1944-production for use and not for profit? We have got neither. The premier goes on to say, "When crop conditions return to normal we shall endeavour to see that those employed in government agencies get any increases which economic conditions permit." Yes, in the light of experience has come profound wisdom to the planners of Saskatchewan.
They talk about raising wages, but adopt a wage freeze in the province of Saskatchewan. I could go on. I think I have said enough, Mr. Speaker, so that you will realize that I intend to vote against the subamendment.
Having dealt with the subamendment I come now to the national situation. What are conditions today? I know that my friends to the left have been predicting depressions and recessions since 1940. As a Canadian I view with great alarm some of the economic conditions with which we in this country find ourselves faced today, but I do not believe in gloating over them. Since as far back as 1950 the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), with his experience and knowledge of public affairs, agriculture and business, and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) as well, have been pointing out the danger signals. This government did not see


them. They did not see the clouds over Washington. These three wise men did not see these things until the other day.
We have been pointing out the danger to our trade for the last seven or eight years. We expressed it when we said we were losing trade in Canada, and that we were losing the British markets. The answer was that we had not lost it, it was still over there. We do not have it. If you know where a thing is you have not lost it.
In 1954 we had the largest unfavourable balance of trade in Canada's history. This is a serious condition. What is being done to meet it? There was a silent, secret pilgrimage to Washington. Where are the policies in the speech from the throne which will meet this situation?
As to agriculture, the farmers are caught between rising costs and falling farm prices. The United States are closing out our barley and oats under quotas, and are threatening to hit our seed growers, and they are now threatening to close out red fescue seed, which is so necessary in parts of western Canada to the agricultural economy. Clover has been closed out, and dairy products. The cost of living is so high today that it makes wheat which is worth $1.40 a bushel at Fort William worth only 53-23 cents a bushel on the farms of western Canada.
Retail sales are going down. In the first ten months of 1954 retail sales were $200 million less. The drop of 14-2 per cent in Saskatchewan sales is caused in part by the serious crop failure there. In Alberta there has been a drop of 7-6 per cent; in Manitoba 4-2 per cent; in Ontario -5 per cent; in Quebec -4 per cent; in British Columbia [DOT]4 per cent. The only part of Canada in which retail sales have increased is the rnari-times, where there has been an increase of [DOT]2 per cent.
What are we doing to meet the situation? What is the reason for it? We have said that over the years Canadians were being taxed out of the markets of the world and taxed out of their jobs. I know they used to say you could make jobs without profits. We have learned differently in Saskatchewan with the disappearance of the mirage of 1944.
What about hidden taxes? The average automobile has a hidden tax of $400. This government in its wisdom has decreed a high cost structure in the last few years. It has isolated our trade. It has started the march of unemployment. I believe that Canada's industry must be revitalized by giving tax relief at once. The government must act and act now.

It is interesting to read the mental peregrinations taken by some of the ministers of the crown with reference to this subject. In September the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said "I can tell you this; taxes won't go up". Then on September 4, 1954, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) said, "I don't think they will go down". As an indication that Saul's change of mind was an amateur performance the Minister of Finance stated on November 15, 1954:
I confess myself concerned about tax rates under which the government takes away half or more of the rewards of hard work which leads to promotion.
I confess myself concerned. Where has he been in recent years? Was he in the department of immigration looking after the shocking practices that were referred to by Mr. McDonald, who was the candidate against the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) in the last federal election? He went on to say this:
There is so much to be gained if we can preserve initiative and enterprise.
He had better talk to the minister of immigration, his successor.
It would be most unfortunate if prospects in this land of opportunity were dimmed by unwise government demands on the fruits of success in business and professional life-indeed in any gainful employment.
That is what we have been saying for long years during which we have had unnecessary taxation. These statements raised hopes. They hinted at tax cuts. They went further than a hint; the people were built up to expectations. Then he went on to say:
From what I have said up to now of my first impressions you might be inclined to infer that I think it is rather a bad show. This is not correct. True, it is awfully large, rates are pretty high, and it is extremely complicated, but withal it appears to me to be a very sensible, well-balanced and flexible tax system.
You just pay your money and you take your choice.
I wish now to speak about the effects of those loose statements. They have had an intense effect on the buying of the Canadian people. In relation to those commodities on which there are excise or other taxes they are postponing purchases. They have done this ever since November. They are waiting. These statements have created uncertainty and instability in a chaotic retail market at a time when retail purchases are falling anyway.
How can it be removed? As I see it, it should be removed at the earliest possible date, by having the budget brought down much earlier than usual. Delay means continued uncertainty such as has prevailed to date, which in turn spells economic instability. The sentiments were laudable, but 50433-13
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker the time at which the statements were made was unfortunate. The result has been serious to the Canadian economy. We hope that the government this session, realizing what the Minister of Finance has at last realized, that high taxation is sapping the power and initiative of the Canadian people, will even at this time do something.
What about the farmers? The agricultural situation in Saskatchewan today is worse than in any other province because of crop failure. The Canadian farmer is caught in a vise-like squeeze between rising prices of what he must buy and falling returns for what he has to sell. In the year 1952-53 our farm prices according to FAO fell by 23 per cent, and retail prices by only 8 per cent. The fall in farm prices has not been transferred to the consumer. Too much of the consumer's dollar finds its way into places other than the farmer's pocket. In the United States in 1951 out of every dollar the farmer received 51 cents. In 1953 he received only 45 cents. My computation makes the Canadian figures even lower than that. Making all allowances for processing, packaging, and things of that sort which are necessary in our modern economy, I come to the conclusion that there is still too great a difference between the price the farmer receives for his commodities and the price paid by the consumer.
What can be done about this? I believe the time has come and indeed is long overdue to investigate this spread, to the end that if there is wrongdoing it will be revealed and punished and if there is not the people of Canada will know the situation.
In the United States the farmer receives 17 per cent of the retail price of tomatoes; 35 per cent of the retail price of potatoes, and 15 per cent of the price of bread. He receives 66 per cent of the price of beef and butter, and 74 per cent of the price of eggs. These percentages are generally duplicated in our country.
The United States has been interfering with our oats and barley market in the U.S.A. I believe the strongest protest should be made to the United States, but not the kind of protest made under the table. I recall one occasion about two years ago when I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) what was being done about it and he said in effect: "We wrote them two letters." I asked, "What was the reply?" He said, in effect: "Why, there was nothing in the letters that demanded a reply."
The United States must realize-and I recognize the tremendous contribution that

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker country is making to the preservation of freedom throughout the world-that it is absolutely necessary that Canada preserve its agricultural productive machine in its present efficiency, and that that can only be attained provided we can export our agricultural products to their country.
Parliament should have an opportunity of making its views clear to the United States. Government ministers trailing to Washington is not enough. They went in silence; they were heard in silence; and they returned in silence. And while this goes on our farm markets are disappearing and our basic industry is fighting a challenge to its very existence.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am going to make one or two suggestions with regard to agriculture and relative to matters that have been brought before parliament on previous occasions. First, I would emphasize that at no time will the people of western Canada allow interference with the Crowsnest rates. Let that be quite clear. What did the government do in this regard? They appointed Chief Justice Sloan, an old friend of theirs and former attorney general of the province of British Columbia. He brought forth the suggestion that these rates were out of date. But no one asked him to do that, unless he was asked in the same secret manner in which our ministers approach the authorities in Washington. I would tell the government that any interference in this connection will be resisted by the western provinces with all the power they command. That agreement was made as a bond; that bond must be maintained.
Our agricultural situation is serious. Our farmers are in a difficult position. I believe the government must bring about a system of cash advances based on a system of wheat storage on the farm. In this regard there is no danger of loss. You will have observed, Mr. Speaker, that in recent years there has been no thefts of wheat in western Canada. Wheat was stolen at one time but now you cannot get a quota book on stolen wheat and therefore that problem has vanished.
Additionally, I believe increased use must be made of the Agricultural Prices Support Act so as to provide adequate support for those commodities to which the act applies. There are support prices on certain commodities but whom do they preserve and protect? They have a peculiar capacity for protecting the packer. In this regard I would again emphasize the suggestion I made a moment ago that a royal commission should


be set up to investigate the price spread between what the farmer receives and the consumer pays.
The next question is: What is to be done about markets? We have embassies all over the world. The United States is selling many of its farm products through the medium of agriculture market officials attached to their embassies. Since we have officials and commissioners stationed all over the world, let us now use them, if we have not already done so, so that it will be their responsibility to carry out the very same tasks United States officials assume and thereby secure a greater share of the markets of the world.
Next, I would call for the establishment of customs facilities at Churchill during that period of the year when the harbour is open so as to encourage the use of the Hudson Bay route.
Finally, I must again urge the government to commence the construction of the South Saskatchewan dam and irrigation project. We were promised it-I think the word was "immediately"-in 1945. The definition of the word "immediately" in so far as the Saskatchewan dam project is concerned closely resembles our understanding of the meaning of eternity. We have waited a long time. We now find that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has been out in western Canada with a draft agreement that has not been accepted by the government. A P.F.R.A. drafted agreement has been shown to the government of Saskatchewan. The Prime Minister says it has no final authority. It is merely the expression of the officials. As a fellow member of the bar, Mr. Speaker, can you imagine a responsible person carrying an agreement around on behalf of somebody else whose authority he has not obtained and the terms of which have not been accepted by the principal? That is exactly the situation here.

I am doing again what I did last year and what I have done before, in that I am taking three years and I am examining the returns for those three years. Our system differs from that in the United States in that they take more than three years. I believe they take four years, away back before the last war began; as a matter of fact before the first war began. They take those figures as a basis for parity, and make a comparison as they go along. At the end of the war, when we set up the Agricultural Prices Support Act, we took the last three years of the war, 1943, 1944 and 1945. Up to that time every farm organization in this country said that was the best condition the farmers had ever lived under up until then. So we took that period and said, "We shall try and maintain the same relationship between costs, as nearly as possible when you take all the products into consideration, as existed in the last three years of the war, not for any one-year period but for the three-year period."
Therefore I am taking the last three years of this period in the sheet I have here. What do I find? I find that the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was right when he said that Saskatchewan had less income from its farms because of crop failure. What is the reduction in income in these three provinces because of wheat reduction in 1954 compared with the. top year in that three year period? Well, in Manitoba it is $83-9 million; in Saskatchewan it is $244-5 million; in Alberta it is $112-4 million. All told it is $440,900,000. The hon. member says we appointed Chief Justice Sloan of British Columbia, who is a good friend of ours, to conduct an inquiry, and he said something about the Crowsnest pass rates. Has he forgotten what the Tories said about the Crowsnest pass rates? They were brought in, as everyone in the country knows, by Sir Wilfrid Laurier when he was in power. He made a deal with the C.P.R. under which the Crowsnest pass rates were established for all time, and his end of the deal has been carried out by succeeding Liberal governments.
When we came to the end of the first war, at which time the Conservatives were in power, what did they do? They moved to do away with the Crowsnest pass agreement, and they would have been successful in doing this had it not been for that chamber which some people criticize so much. On that occasion when the members of this house had not been here for a sufficient length of time to remember all that is attached to the Crowsnest pass agreement, the then prime minister, the leader of the Conservative party, who was a member from the province of Manitoba which has gained as

In spite of what he did, in spite of the objections he raised and in spite of the objections raised right across the country, actions were taken which did away with much of the effectiveness of the Crowsnest rates.
What happened? When the Liberals came back into power in 1921 they appointed a commission, such as the one my hon. friend has been asking us to appoint for other reasons now, and had them look into the whole thing. As a result of the activities of that commission in 1927, you still have the Crowsnest rates and had your maritime rates established. Why? As an alternative to the Crowsnest pass rates on our grain being shipped through. I am satisfied that if we were to get up in this house and argue in favour of taking off the Crowsnest pass rates, at the same time we would be asking to take off the special rates that have been given in connection with maritime freight.
Any group attempting to do that, I do not care whether they sat over there or over here, would not be here after the next election. Therefore when my hon. friend points his long finger at us and indicates what we ought to do, he should read about what his own party has done. If he has any appeals to make on that question he should make them to the men who are sitting behind him, not to the men sitting over here. I would suggest that so far as that question is concerned there are certain things which can and will be said as we go along and discuss the question from time to time.

I will repeat what I said before, namely there is no one in this house or outside who is more anxious than I to get the South Saskatchewan river dam started. But if anyone goes out to Saskatchewan and states that this government has not been doing what ought to be done in the interests of the western people, and particularly the western farmers, then I wish to state that the figures I have given contradict that assertion. In so far as the government is concerned, and in so far as the house from which all financial proposals originate is concerned, we can substantiate every single dollar of expenditure that has been made. I am quite satisfied that in due course there will be support for further amounts, and all I am asking at the moment is that we exercise a little patience.
It has been suggested that we have already shown enough patience, but I would point out that everyone in this house is agreed on this project, and I have never known a project which had the unanimous support of the house which was not eventually undertaken. I would therefore suggest to hon. members that when they speak on this topic they make it plain to the people of Canada that we are fully aware of the need for this dam. Let it not be suggested that the government is not going to do it and that it should therefore be forgotten-. Let us get busy at the task of proving why we want this dam and why it will be good for Canada as a whole.
Let us not suggest, as did the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) a few

moments ago, that this is merely an irrigation scheme. No government could possibly build a dam at such a cost merely for the purpose of irrigating 400,000 acres of land. In addition, that sort of appeal will not weigh with the people in eastern Canada, or even in central Canada. The water at the dam will be 185 feet deep, and in actual fact the top ten feet of that water can be run off by gravity in order to irrigate the 400,000 acres of land and affect the income on millions of acres. The people should also know that once the dam is put there we will have a lake 145 miles long, or three-quarters of the length of lake Erie or lake Ontario. The water behind that dam will not only irrigate the land but will create a huge head of power which can be used right across the province of Saskatchewan and if necessary on into other provinces both east and west.
This same problem was dealt with yesterday at a meeting in Kansas. I heard a gentleman get up and tell the people that they had to conserve their water, and they had to make greater use of their available streams than they were doing at the present time. On my flight across the state of Missouri afterward I saw dugouts on every farm, the same kind of thing we have out in the provinces of Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba. When we view that sort of situation we should remember that as a result of the building of this dam we are going to provide many benefits for western communities, including water for industries. There will be water supply for scores of towns which are below the level of the dam.
In conclusion I would say to hon. members of this house that if they get that idea over to the Canadian people, then there is no doubt in my mind as to what eventually will be done.

speechtext:
Certainly any planning the Conservative party ever did in Saskatchewan has been a horrible experience, and I was surprised the hon. member did not admit that he was to all intents and purposes a voice crying in the wilderness as far as that party in Saskatchewan is concerned.
We have heard many speeches over the past few days, and in most cases the speakers have voiced the opinion that the speech from the throne provides hon. members with an opportunity of bringing to the attention of parliament those matters which are of the greatest concern to their own constituents. I think that is understandable, but I also believe that if we are going to discharge our duties as members of parliament we must not forget that we represent all the people of Canada. I know it is hard to see the other fellow's point of view; it is hard to see the other fellow's problems. But if we are going to properly assess our own problems in our own areas, I am convinced that we must have a fairly good working knowledge of the many and varied types of occupations and industries in this country. I think more people than ever before realize that we must have a good working knowledge of all phases of endeavour in this vast country of ours. If I speak, as I probably shall this afternoon, with respect to agriculture in this country, I do so with the idea of trying to relate it to the whole Canadian economy.
Last summer I took the opportunity of visiting for a month or six weeks in eastern Canada, the maritimes and, I may say for the benefit of my French-Canadian friends across the way, the province of Quebec. It was a wonderful experience. I gained a great deal of knowledge as to the difficulties and the problems that are being faced in other parts of Canada. I should like to take this opportunity of inviting members from eastern Canada and the maritimes who have not recently visited western Canada to go out there and see at first hand some of the difficulties and problems with which we are faced.
We hear a great deal, Mr. Speaker, about the proposition of one world; we hear a great deal about a world community. In the minds of most people I think it means something more than just a geographical proposition. I think it means the peoples of all countries living together in a sort of brotherhood based on the principles laid down in the Atlantic charter. I will be the first to admit that when we look at the situation that exists in the world today, it does not sound too realistic. However, I am convinced that it is the goal

The Address-Mr. Bryson toward which we must all strive. I am convinced that we have no choice but to accept that principle.
If we are going to condition our thinking to this idea of one world, I think the best thing we can do is to start at home, because Canada also has become a very small community, as will be acknowledged by anybody who takes a look at our transportation system or our communications system and who gives any consideration to the economy of this country.
More people than ever before realize that in any small community such as Canada has become, you cannot have one segment of our economy depressed and another segment of it fairly prosperous. Nor can you have one section of our people unemployed and on relief and another section of our people enjoying comparative prosperity. Those two conditions cannot exist in a community.
They cannot exist in Canada for another reason, too. We cannot afford to have conditions such as those I have outlined if we are going to attempt to set an example to the hundreds of millions of people in other parts of the world who are looking around, standing in the shadow, trying to make up their minds as to just what their choice is going to be as between the two dominant political philosophies that we find in the world today.
These conditions do exist in this country, Mr. Speaker, as is quite evident. Daily it is becoming increasingly more difficult for workers to exchange the product of their labour and their ingenuity for a better standard of living; and by the same token it is becoming increasingly more difficult for agricultural producers to market the food which they produce. I contend that food is the most important commodity on earth.
If we are going to consider this Canadian agricultural scene, I believe it is time we faced up to a few of the hard facts of life in connection with it. I think it is time we believed that Canadian agriculture, in so far as the welfare of the Canadian people is concerned, is the greatest industry we have. I believe it is one of the greatest industries we have because so many other industries are dependent on it.
In the corridor here the other day a member of the house said to me: "Yes, I will admit that the farm machinery industry is suffering a mild recession. I will even go so far as to admit that there are production slow-downs. I will even go so far as to say there are work stoppages; but you are not going to condemn the system just on the ground that one industry in this vast country is suffering economic distress." But what my hon. friend did not realize was the

fact that the farm machinery industry in this country does not produce a finished machine. What about the workers in the rubber industry, who put the tires on these implements? What about the people engaged in the manufacture of batteries? What about the people who manufacture bearings, paint, ignition systems, generators, starters, spark plugs and lighting equipment? When you have a production slow-down or work stoppage in this important industry, you have a corresponding work stoppage and production slow-down in a great many other industries. The same thing applies also to the automotive industry.
I think we in Canada are stuck with this agricultural industry. I think we are stuck with it because of our large amount of arable land, because of our climate and because of our people. By people in other parts of the world we are going to be looked upon as one of the greatest food producers, in so far as our export is concerned, in the world. In all probability we are destined to play that important role, just as we have played it in the past. Therefore we must make up our minds as to what kind of agricultural industry we want in this country. Do we want an industry like the one we had in the thirties, a sort of twentieth century peasantry? Or do we want in this country an agricultural industry that is prosperous, one that will make for general prosperity not only among our own people but which, if it is properly distributed, will provide for the world food which in my opinion is still the greatest force mankind has ever invented to ensure the peace of the world.
In spite of the things we have heard from the Minister of Agriculture let us not delude ourselves that agriculture is in a healthy position. It must be admitted that western Canada suffered a tremendous crop failure in 1954. That crop represents only a fraction of the normal. As far as Saskatchewan is concerned, it is estimated that our income will be reduced by $250 million this year. This means that the purchasing power of the people of the province will be reduced by approximately 45 per cent as compared with last year, and in some parts of my constituency the figure will run as high as 80 per cent. But once again let us not forget that in the last three years the farmers of western Canada have grown five crops. Let nobody say that the economic distress western Canada is now experiencing is the result of the short and disastrous crop we had last summer, because we in western Canada have grown five normal crops in three years.
Many people say, "If you have done this, how is it that you find yourselves in this position today?" According to dominion bureau of statistics figures, since 1951 the

prices that farmers throughout Canada have received for what they sold have gone down eight points while their costs have risen 14 points. In my own province farmers' costs have risen 16 points, which means that so far as their net income is concerned they are 24 points worse off than they were three years ago.
I wonder how many other Canadian businesses could remain solvent faced with this kind of thing. Yet the farmers are asked and expected to go on producing under these conditions. They are even told now that in all probability their net income will be further reduced next year. Of course this evil day has only been postponed because of the fact that we have grown five crops in three years, yet many people will try to make themselves believe that other factors are responsible.
A great deal has been said about unemployment, but I do not intend to say too much about it. Some say that in the next month or two there will be 600,000 unemployed. Some go so far as to say that there will be 750,000. This condition has arisen because of the loss of purchasing power of the primary producer. The primary producer is not buying as many goods and services as he formerly did because he does not have the purchasing power to do so. When he does not purchase the manufacturer slows down production. When he slows down production he lays off men. When he lays off men their incomes are not as large as they were, so they do not buy as many consumer goods as they did. This brings about a further slow-down of production with a further lay-off of workers. So you have the whole process repeated over and over again.
I think it is time we stopped trying to make ourselves believe that the situation will cure itself if we give it enough time. There are a great many things that I believe we could do. The Minister of Agriculture has told us over and over again that the people of Canada provide the best market for the things produced in Canada. Let us take a look at that statement. Maybe he has something there. We have 600,000 unemployed. One does not have to be much of a mathematician to realize that 600,000 unemployed could represent about a million and a half people in Canada who are not eating quite as much as they did before, who are not purchasing quite as many clothes as they did before. Why not take a look at this potential market? Let us put these people to work.
As far as markets are concerned, I saw a report the other day that the Soviet union is going to import 240 million pounds of
The Address-Mr. Bryson meat products this year. Last year Canada Packers made a deal to sell pork to Russia, and got an export permit from the government. I cannot see any difference in the government making a deal to sell meat to Russia this year. I believe that market should be investigated.
But I think the crux of the situation lies in the fact that the government should do what they had in mind in 1945 when they called the dominion-provincial conference on reconstruction. At that time they had in mind that if and when unemployment or a depression appeared in Canada they would undertake a public works and public investment program. Of course such a public investment program was contingent on a designated number of provinces signing a dominion-provincial tax agreement. That has happened. The way is clear.
I maintain, as other members have emphasized in previous speeches, that this is the time for the government of Canada to undertake a public works program. Once they have done so it is my view that they should call a dominion-provincial conference to decide where these public works projects should be built to produce the best results. As was pointed out yesterday, as far as anything built in western Canada is concerned 75 per cent of the money involved in the cost of such projects will accrue to interests in eastern Canada and 25 per cent will remain in the west.
I believe, too, that the South Saskatchewan river dam should be constructed. I think that is one of the more important public investments that could be made. Somebody said they believed that the Minister of Agriculture wants the dam. I honestly believe he wants the dam. For all I know it may be that he is a captive of the Liberal party, but I should like him to come out of that captivity and build the dam. I am sure that if the dam is built we will all be happy, and in all probability we will call it the Gardiner dam.
I said we should put people to work on public projects. If war came tomorrow we would put these people to work. There is no question but that we need many things in Canada. We need more hospitals. We need a road-building program of the type indicated the other evening by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch). All these things would in themselves be wealth-creating and largely self-liquidating. In my opinion such a program is the only thing that would approach a solution to this problem. Such a program is being sought by a great many responsible organizations in

The Address-Mr. Bryson Canada. It is being requested by the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities and by labour organizations. It is even being asked for by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.
I should like to spend a few minutes discussing a problem about which I am very much concerned and have been very much concerned for a long time. I refer to the problem of Indian affairs. One does not have to study the Indian affairs branch long before it becomes pretty obvious that the same kind of bungling goes on in that department that goes on in a great many other government departments. It is my sincere hope that the new Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, whose department deals with Indian affairs, will give a great deal of serious consideration to the problem, and will show much more enthusiasm in an attempt to come up with solutions to a few of these Indian problems than any of his predecessors have shown in the past. I have to admit that many procedures have become so well established in that branch that I doubt if even the new minister will have very much success in finding a solution. But there are a great many urgent problems to be solved.
Before mentioning some of them I should like for a moment to take a look at the reserves system. About 70 years ago the government of Canada undertook to place the Indians on reserves. I assume that in the back of their minds they believed that this system of reserves would be a means to an end, and I hope the end was assimilation. I believe that is correct. And I also believe that the reserves system was the most infamous and most immoral thing any one group of people ever imposed upon another group. We who profess freedom in this country, and laud to high heaven the dignity of man, rounded up these primitive people and put them in compounds with just about as much compunction as we do the buffalo. We denied them the white man's privileges. And while we restricted their association with white people we exploited them at every turn, inflicting upon these comparatively happy and self-sufficient people all the vices and diseases of the white man, until in the majority of cases we have completely demoralized them.
In other words we used just about every conceivable device to guarantee the failure of assimilation. And after 50 years of experience this government is now contemplating setting up more of these infamous reserves. Yes, it is going out and buying land for that purpose. I read a report-I hope it is not true, because I am not prepared to believe

it-that they are even considering setting up some kind of reserves system for the metis people in this country. God forbid!
I should like to tell a story about what is going on in one reserve in my constituency, and there are others in a similar position. There is no Indian agent within a hundred miles. If one of these Indians wants to sell a cord of wood, a bushel of wheat or a few fence posts he has to hitch-hike a hundred miles there and a hundred miles home to obtain written permission from the Indian agent to dispose of that product. The obvious result is that he does not do this.
About a month ago the local papers throughout the area were circulating a request for clothing and food to alleviate what they described as a deplorable condition among the Indians. I hope the minister is going to investigate that very serious situation. I would like to bring to his attention the serious position of the northern Indians in this country and suggest to him- I am sorry he is not in his seat-that he make a very careful examination of the personnel working in the field for the Indian affairs branch. I will be the first to admit that a great many of them have all the outward appearances of possessing the qualifications necessary for their work, but there are factors involved with many of them, factors which I do not wish to put on Hansard because some of these people are friends of mine, which render them utterly useless in the job they are now doing.

speechtext:
No, they are not Liberals. I would be happy to give the minister in private what I refrain from saying in the house respecting these people.
The Department of National Health and Welfare has gone into the north country, augmented by the health services of the different provinces, and has brought about a situation under which the Indian population is increasing rapidly. I find that in one area the infant mortality rate has dropped from eighteen to three per thousand of population. That is a wonderful improvement. But here you have the perfectly silly situation of spending the taxpayers' money in providing a service and at the same time allowing conditions to exist which make these people the complete and absolute wards of the government, in a most disgraceful manner.
Let me illustrate. We still believe we are going to be able to assimilate these people, so we say they have to go to school; and here is where I say the department falls down in its administration. They pay the Indians family allowances-and I hope no one will

get the impression that I am opposed to family allowances, because I am not. I would like to see everybody, including the Indians, get family allowances. But I certainly take objection to the administration of those payments.
Here is what happens; here is why I say the men in the field are inefficient. They are paying these Indians family allowances, but at the same time they say, "In order to collect your family allowance cheques you have to send your children to school." What does that mean? If these men knew their business they would know that was not a proper thing to do. An Indian family is a unit. If one member goes, they all go. They sit around the posts now, collecting their family allowances. The cheques are taken in to the Hudson's Bay Company-these exploiters who have learned well their trade over two hundred years-and do the Indians buy essentials with these family allowance cheques? No, they do not. These are primitive people; they are buying ribbons and Mickey Mouse watches, and the Hudson's Bay Company could not care less. Why should they? They are in business. Free enterprise!
So, Mr. Speaker, the end result, with one exception which I shall mention later, is that the Indians are not going out on the trapping grounds in the winter nor are they going out fishing in the summer. They cannot, because the Indian woman has to stay and look after the children. They have to go to school if the Indian family is to receive the family allowance payments. And the Indian man cannot go out and do anything without the woman, because she does the work.
Let us get down to the facts. I say there is something desperately wrong with the administration of that department when conditions like that are allowed to exist. But there is one exception. Some bright boy on the Indian field staff came up with this idea. The trapping season starts on December 15, so we will let these Indians go out on the trap lines between December 15 and March 15. How utterly stupid are those people. Anyone who has had experience in the north country knows that trapping is a quite considerable business. You cannot say, "I am going out to trap tomorrow." You have to say about the middle of August that you are going out to itrap, and you get ready for December 15. Again this is a sample of maladministration.
I say the government of Canada is spending the taxpayers' money to create a condition whereby the Indian population is increasing, and at the same time it is allowing a condition to develop under which these people are
The Address-Mr. Bryson becoming wards of the government. I would suggest that the government establish trading stores in the north. Let us forget about this Hudson's Bay Company. Let the government provide trading stores in the north where they will sell essential things to the Indians in exchange for the family allowance.
That may be a kind of shock treatment, but the government is using a little bit of shock treatment on these people now, and I condone it. I believe the government was completely justified last year when it took a team of X-ray specialists into that country. To the Indians, of course, that was a kind of bogeyman. They did not want to be X-rayed. So the specialist said, "All right; no X-ray, no treaty." That is what I call the shock treatment. I think it was all right. In that particular respect the means justified the end. I suggest they set up government stores in the north where those Indians can buy essentials, flour instead of ribbons and sugar instead of Mickey Mouse watches.
