I maintain that the welfare of the Indians of this country rests primarily on the people who are administering family allowances.
I almost hesitate to do this, but I am going to commend the government on setting up locker plants in the north where the Indians can store meat against hard times, with Indian participation financially. Of course I hope we never again have a repetition of what happened last summer at one place in the north where, after the meat was stored in the plant and the summer came along, with Indians all around the post-they cannot go away; if they do they do not collect the family allowance, so they stay at the post-the man in charge of the locker plant decided he was going on a two months' holiday and took the key with him, leaving the Indians in a state of complete panic and near famine. I hope that will be investigated by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. I hope they set up more of these lockers.
I have a suggestion now for the minister that I believe will bring about a solution,

The Address-Mr. Blackmore
possibly more rapidly than anything else I know of. I urge the government to call a dominion-provincial conference at the earliest possible moment in an effort to work out a long-term financial agreement with the provinces, so the provinces may take over the administration of Indian affairs in this country. I believe that would be a step in the right direction, on the ground that the provinces individually would be much better able to cope with this situation.
Those closely associated with Indians believe that is the ultimate solution. The present policy is inadequate, and what is more important it is completely unrealistic. Certainly we as a people who profess all the Christian ethics associated with a free people in a democracy can no longer go around shutting our eyes and turning our backs on these unfortunate people who, through no fault of their own, have become the victims of our refusal to accept and treat them as deserving citizens within our country.
I think, after what I have said, Mr. Speaker, you will agree that I do not intend to support the motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is generally agreed among authorities that mankind has solved the problem of production, but that mankind has not solved the problem of distribution. It is not, perhaps, adequately realized and appreciated that in this age of machines and wonderworking skills man must solve the problem of distribution or face probable extinction from the earth. One of the amazing things to me is that for years and years now our government has done nothing, so far as I can see, to develop or discover a method of distribution any different from what their forefathers were using in 1895.
For freedom-loving men the only potentially satisfactory method of distribution is the financial philosophy and mechanism of Social Credit. What mankind must have is the means whereby men can make what is physically possible financially possible. As the clearest evidence that we have not yet accomplished that objective, it is well known to everyone that just as soon as we develop more of a particular kind of goods than the people are buying, the price of those goods goes down and down and the people producing those goods are worse off than they were when there was a scarcity of goods, which shows quite clearly that up to the present time we have nothing even resembling a scientific method of distribution or a scientific method of making that which is physically possible financially possible.
The financial technique of Social Credit provides a means whereby man can make what is physically possible financially pos-

sible, not only in producing goods from the resources available but in consuming the goods already produced.
The Social Credit financial technique comprises three elements. These elements are: one, the free flow of credit; two, the just price; three, a national dividend to be paid to every qualified member of the community or society. Regardless, Mr. Speaker, of what mischievous organs like the Winnipeg Free Press and others are endeavouring to mislead the people into believing as being what Social Credit advocates, the statements which I have made here are correct.
May we briefly consider each of these three elements. Let us take first the free flow of credit. Through establishing and maintaining a free flow of credit a society or state, without increase of debt, of taxation or of prices, is able to make available to itself whatever money is necessary to bring about and sustain whatever measure or degree of prosperity its resources render possible, avoiding both depressions and undesirable booms; depressions, as we know, resulting from too little money coming into the markets to buy goods offered for sale; booms or inflationary periods resulting from too much money coming into the markets to buy such goods.
Now, where is it supposed a government in a Social Credit society is to obtain the money required to establish and maintain this free flow of credit? It is a certain thing that no government we have ever had in Ottawa, in the Dominion of Canada, and no government they have had in Washington in the United States, has ever been able to establish a free flow of credit with the devices they have used.
Now to explain where the money could come from. Let us recall that the constitutions of both Canada and the United States empower the government to create the nation's money just as actually the royal mint at Ottawa stamps out Canadian coins, nickels, dimes, quarters and fifty cent pieces. The Canadian constitution, the British North America Act, under section 91 gives the parliament of Canada exclusive legislative jurisdiction over, first, currency and coinage under subsection 14; second, banking, the incorporation of banks and the issue of paper money under subsection 15; and third, legal tender under subsection 20. These three powers are all that are required to enable the government of Canada to create in Canada all the money which the resources and the production of Canada will justify.
The United States constitution, article I, section 8, paragraph 5, states in part:
Congress shall have power to coin money and regulate the value thereof.

What use has Canada made of this constitutional power thus vested in her federal government? We have had two or three cases in which successful attempts have been made. Under the Finance Act of 1914 the Canadian minister of finance, Sir Thomas White, created scores and even hundreds of millions of Canadian dollars. In the period from 1914 to 1917 he created $26 million Canadian and spent them in the conduct of the war. They were not funny money either, nor rubber dollars. We will find the record of what I have just said on page 22 of the report of the royal commission on banking and currency in Canada, published in 1933.
In 1917 Sir Thomas White created $50 million and used it to buy Canadian grain and other products for Britain, those dollars being backed up by imperial treasury bills. An account of this transaction will be found at page 22 of the report to which I have referred already. Altogether he created more than $1,200 million Canadian during world war I and advanced it to Britain to purchase in Canada foodstuffs, munitions and other products for the conduct of world war I. This will be found recorded at page 85 of the report of the royal commission on banking and currency in Canada.
Sir Thomas White, in his memorandum of dissent signed at Ottawa on October 3, 1933, as reported at page 85 of the report, positively declared.
But there was on the part of the government no "policy of inflation."
It is a favourite lie used by Liberals and Conservatives all over Canada to speak of Social Credit and its use of government money as inflation. I suppose the C.C.F. do a similar thing because they do not hesitate to do all the things the other two parties do. A Social Credit government in Canada could, and most likely would, obtain money to maintain the free flow of credit from exactly the same sources that supplied Sir Thomas White with much of the money with which he financed Canada's relatively colossal war effort in world war I.
Canada's finance minister, Sir Thomas White, through the use of a specialized financial agency entitled the Finance Act of 1914, created the Canadian dollars he needed, first, to stimulate the development of Canadian production of goods and services and, second, to market those goods and services to advantage. A Social Credit government in Canada, likewise through the use of a specialized financial agency, a national monetary commission, would create the Canadian dollars needed, first, to stimulate Canadian production in accordance with the desires of Canadians; second, to enable Canadian producers to market their production and, third,
The Address-Mr. Blackmore to enable Canadian consumers to obtain and enjoy that production, attaining an ever and ever higher standard of living and of security.
Everyone today is wondering about the tremendous impact which the discovery and employment of atomic power is going to have on the production of goods. Everyone is realizing the almost appalling efficiency of great modern machines such as those described, if I remember rightly, by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) last night. Surely everyone must be concerned about what is going to happen as a result of the enormous increase in production unless some means are developed whereby the people will be able to partake of the production after it is brought into existence.
Anyone who takes the time to be realistic at all knows that it will be utterly impossible to obtain money by taxation with which to enable the people to buy the goods produced by these great machines and through these remarkable technological skills. We might just as well face that fact and be honest. Every one of us should remember that when he is out on the platform talking to the people. The time has come when the people of Canada have a right to be told the truth, no matter what it is, by the man standing on the platform.

Mr. Speaker, before the house took recess I was discussing the Social Credit free flow of credit proposal, and how money would be obtained with which to support the free flow of credit. I pointed out that the method whereby Social Crediters would obtain money would closely resemble the method whereby Sir Thomas White obtained millions of dollars through the application of the Finance Act of 1914 in conducting world war I. I pointed out there need be no more question of the soundness of Social Credit money than there was concerning the money which Sir Thomas White used on that occasion.
Opponents of Social Credit contend that a Social Credit government's money would be unsound. "Funny money," they like to call it. But would they dare to suggest that the dollars issued under the Finance Act of 1914 were unsound? Would they suggest those dollars were funny? I think not.
What makes the Canadian dollar sound inside Canada? Is it gold? Many people think so, but it is not. It is goods and services

The Address-Mr. Blackmore backed by Canadian resources, material and human, standing ready to produce and to deliver more goods and services. An excellent working definition of the dollar is this; "a dollar is a ticket to goods." Such being the case, the number of dollars the Minister of Finance could safely issue within the Canadian economy would be roughly related to the amount of goods offered for sale within Canadian markets.
Another helpful definition of a dollar is that "a dollar is a medium of exchange." Bearing this definition in mind we must recognize that the number of dollars going into Canadian markets ought to be related to the number of exchanges Canadians would be able and willing to make with each other.
These two considerations enable anyone who desires to do so to form a concrete means of judging whether there might be too much money within an economy at any given time. Sir Thomas White's Finance Act dollars were unquestionably sound because their number was consciously geared to Canadian goods and services available for the exchanges Canadians wished to make.
Opponents of Social Credit argue that under a Social Credit administration there would be issued too many dollars; "turning on the printing presses", they derisively call it. But the Social Crediters would exercise adequate caution in issuing currency and credit, both debt money to be loaned into circulation and debt-free money to be spent. Social Crediters know the fundamental facts about money, just as did Sir Thomas White. Would any informed and honest man disparagingly accuse Sir Thomas White of "turning on the printing presses"? I do not believe that expression was used in Canada until it became in the interests of certain political people to discredit Social Credit.
Opponents of Social Credit have always endeavoured to show that it would establish a dictatorship. But quite the contrary is the case. Social Credit would establish the freest state and the most fully democratic government the mind of man can conceive. Did Sir Thomas White establish a dictatorship in developing and employing the Finance Act of 1914? Even to ask that question is to be unfair to his memory and to shock almost any hon. member into serious thought.
The opponents of Social Credit will ask: "How could prices be maintained without iron controls?" I think it was the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew), speaking some time ago in connection with Social Credit, who asked that question. The answer is that prices on the whole would be maintained by a scientific use of the law of supply and


demand. It is the law of supply and demand that is supposed to affect prices today. By having and exercising ready, effective control over financial policy the Minister of Finance would be readily able to increase the supply of almost any commodity in Canada, thereby dealing with the tendency of prices to rise.
Some will ask, "But how could he increase the supply quickly enough to offset an inflationary tendency?" After a Social Credit government had been in operation for a certain length of time we would find that it would probably have on hand a considerable supply of many commodities, just as we find today the dominion government of Canada has on hand a considerable supply of butter, eggs, and other commodities.
I have stated several times in this house that it would be greatly in the interests of this nation to store up a good supply of different kinds of grain, sugar, honey, and other commodities of that nature so there would be reserves available in case a need arises to free certain commodities upon the market when there appears to be sufficient shortage to cause a price rise.
The Minister of Finance could manage tendencies toward falling prices by a policy of price support wherever necessary, much as we are doing in Canada today through the agricultural prices support program. He could buy and take temporary control of and withdraw from the market all unmanageable surpluses, especially of non-perishable goods such as wheat, sugar, and so forth. As I have already indicated, we have followed such a policy in Canada, and in fact we are doing so now. We had a number of similar policies during world war II. However, the device has not been used, shall I say, wholesale or all across the board, or in a general way for the purpose of being able to control prices in this country.
No one would speak of devices such as I have indicated as being "iron controls" unless he was having a nightmare. Depressions and booms could be controlled and practically eliminated by the use of Social Credit financial measures. To go into sufficient detail to establish that thesis would, of course, require far more time than is available either to anyone speaking in this house or to hon. members listening. One has simply to study the whole science of Social Credit with a desire to learn the truth concerning it.
At the same time these measures I have indicated would be used, there would be, as potent aids to the Minister of Finance in his endeavour to control prices both deflationary and inflationary, two other Social Credit financial devices, namely the just price and the national dividend. The just price is obtained

or determined quite scientifically by reference to two considerations. The first is that the aim would be to give the producer the cost of production plus a just profit. The other would be to use what is called the just price factor. I have not time to go into the details pertaining to that matter, but it is fully understood by those who endeavour to learn. The just price factor would enable those managing the economy to determine what should be the compensated discount on prices to bring them down to the place where they ought to be. There would be no dictatorship, no iron controls involved. In fact I think we would find that a large percentage of the control would be exercised by the various elements in society itself.
The labour unions are exercising more and more influence in the conduct of the affairs of the nation, and they are going to do so in the days to come. As they realize that they have more and more responsibility for their own well-being as well as for the wellbeing of all other members of the state, we shall find that they will become far more enlightened and purposeful in all their moves. They will play a considerable part, I believe, in determining economic policy, much as they are doing today.
The Canadian Manufacturers Association are also exercising a potent influence. Other elements of society will exercise a potent influence too, and in due time they will find that, rather than fighting each other, it will be greatly to their advantage to sit around a council table, talk matters over and decide how big the pie is that is to be divided up and how large a part each of them ought to have, and proceed to determine a means whereby each can obtain his equitable share. This is not at all beyond the realm of possibility. In fact even today proposals are being made which are rather far-reaching. One of them was referred to last night by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart).
The national dividend is a means of introducing into the economy of the nation enough purchasing power to enable the people consuming to buy the produce which is on the market. That is, if it is discovered that there is a surplus, issuing the national dividend would be another means of absorbing that surplus and preventing it from causing a fall in prices. Surely anyone who desires to face facts-as I am sure every member of this house today realizes we must-ought to be able to see that there is no element of dictatorship in all of those measures.

Mr. Speaker, according to the latest figures produced jointly by the dominion bureau of

The Address-Mr. Hees statistics and the federal Department of Labour, unemployment in November last was 42 per cent greater than in November of the year before. Each month in the past year we have seen a very marked increase in unemployment over the corresponding month of the year before; but, hard as it is to believe, despite these facts there is no indication whatsoever in the speech from the throne that this government has any plans for correcting the basic causes of unemployment.
In the speech from the throne suggestions are made that changes will be made in the Unemployment Insurance Act, and in fact yesterday we passed a bill which made some necessary changes, which have been suggested for two or three years past by the official opposition, increasing the rates of supplementary benefits and extending the minimum period of payment.
The government also suggested in the speech from the throne that the public works program would be accelerated; but, as I have said, despite the fact that in every month of the past year unemployment was a great deal higher than in the corresponding month of the year before, there appears to be no indication whatsoever of any plans which this government has for correcting the basic causes of unemployment. It seems that this government intends to persist in its policy of "hope and grope" for the answers which it never does seem to find.
We must ask ourselves whether we are going to look at this thing constructively. What are the reasons we are experiencing considerably more unemployment than a year ago? I believe there are two main reasons. First of all, we may as well face the fact that producers in other countries are beating Canadian producers in price or design or both. They are moving into our domestic and export markets, and their products are receiving ready acceptance among buyers who formerly were quite content to buy Canadian products.
I believe the second reason is the high taxes we are paying. These have added considerably to the selling price of the goods we produce, and are helping very materially to price our goods out of both the domestic and the export market. In addition to the high commodity taxes, the high income taxes that we are all required to pay are making it increasingly difficult for people to buy the goods we are offering for sale. Tonight I should like to examine each of these causes in turn.
First of all, let us have a look at what other countries are doing to lower their costs and improve their designs so that their

steadily increasing sales make it possible for them to take advantage of mass production methods, which in turn lead to lower costs and enable them to sell more and more goods in competition with us in both our domestic and our export markets. These increasing sales of other countries are the main reason Canadian workmen are being laid off and going on short time.
In order to get some idea of what other countries are actually doing, it is only necessary to take a look at their production figures. Take, for instance, Britain. Despite the fact that Great Britain had to make a complete conversion from wartime to peacetime production, Great Britain is turning out 175 per cent of her production in 1938. Despite the fact that West Germany had to rebuild from the rubble of 1945, today that country is producing 170 per cent of the total production of all Germany in 1938. That will give the house some idea of the kind of production effort that is going on in Europe today. The same story is true in varying degrees in France, Italy, Switzerland, Belgium and Holland, and it gives us some idea of the kind of competition we are up against.
Because of the need for those countries to replace a great deal of their industrial plant, they have had of necessity to put in a great many new machine tools. Thus they are able to produce a wide variety of new designs in almost every type of production they have embarked upon. Their almost unbelievable urge to rebuild and produce at the same time has made them willing to work long hours and increase their efficiency to a point where their costs, in almost every instance, are well below ours.
One of the main factors, Mr. Speaker, in this tremendous industrial progress in Europe, in fact also in Japan and in the United States, has been industrial research, aimed at discovering new products and developing new designs and more efficient methods of production. These industrial research programs which have been carried on in these countries have been undertaken on a very large and important scale, and I think it is obvious to every one of us that if we here in Canada are going to keep pace with our competitors, we must embark on a research program of a comparable nature.
It was with this in mind that, at the last session, the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) introduced a resolution urging this government to set up a committee which would include representatives of management, labour and the educational institutions, and would examine the possibilities, and best means of operation, of a greatly

expanded industrial research program. In its work this committee would be guided very largely by the experience in Great Britain and the United States in setting up similar committees, and developing similar programs. But though this suggestion was favourably commented upon by newspapers of every political leaning in almost every part of this country, and though it was favourably commented upon by industrial and labour leaders from coast to coast, this government turned it down.
It did it by very skilfully seeing to it that on a certain day, at a certain time when this measure was to come up for discussion, private members' bills and resolutions were cut oif just before this resolution was due to come forward. This was not just by chance. It was, I believe, because this government knew this resolution was something it could not afford to vote against, and it simply could not bear to see a good and a very much needed measure brought in by the opposition with the opposition receiving credit for it. So, despite the fact that this measure was badly needed, the government, I believe, saw to it that it could not be brought forward.
This year the hon. member for Lambton West has introduced the same resolution; and though I am sorry to see that the government did not have the good sense to introduce this as a measure of its own in the speech from the throne, I hope they will at least allow this measure to come forward this year, and will vote for and adopt it.
The second matter with which I would like to deal tonight is the question of high taxes which are making it very difficult, if not impossible, for certain of our products to be sold both in the domestic and the export markets. This government has always taken the attitude that if you reduce taxes you will lose tax revenue. I say that is by no means necessarily correct, and a very good example of this was shown in the case of the cigarette tax a couple of years ago. The government materially raised the tax, and the consumption of cigarettes dropped off so badly that the total tax revenue decreased to such an extent that the government had to lower the tax again. Then the consumption of cigarettes went up again and the tax intake was restored. If this government will adopt a sensible policy of reducing commodity taxes materially, more of these commodities will be sold, and I believe the total tax revenue will very likely be as great as, or perhaps even greater, than it was before.
Another thing which this government can do is to materially reduce the income tax,
The Address-Mr. Hees because a reduction in the income tax will make it possible for more people to buy more goods. Because of the increased consumption of goods, I believe the loss in tax revenue can easily be made up by more people being employed in producing goods and thereby earning incomes on which they will pay tax, instead of drawing on the government in the form of unemployment insurance benefits. I believe these tax reductions will make it possible to sell more products both in the domestic and the export markets, and will go a long way toward putting a great many of our workmen back at work.
And now, I would like to give an example of how I think industrial research can help establish a new industry. I am going to speak tonight about the potential oil and gas industry in western Canada. We all know that in Alberta, and to a lesser extent in British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, we have enormous reserves of gas and oil. In recent years more than $5 billion worth of these reserves have been proved, and we know these are only a small fraction of the reserves which are confidently believed to be present in these areas.
If the incentive for exploration is continued by opening up additional markets, and if that expansion is accompanied by a comprehensive and continued program of industrial research to develop better techniques for processing oil and gas products, I believe we can develop a by-product industry which will be of tremendous importance to western Canada. This will lead to the building of literally dozens of sulphur, chemical, and petrochemical plants, which will require hundreds of millions of dollars worth of capital investment, and will create employment for many, many thousands of Canadians.
In addition to this by-product industry, this would lead to the development in western Canada of a very important steel industry which would use Canadian iron ore as well as coal and gas, and could produce steel pipe and steel casings to be used in thousands of miles of Canadian oil lines across the prairie provinces, and in many Canadian oil wells.
Another example of what research might do to lead to the greater utilization of raw materials would be the development of a more efficient method of producing by-products and hydroelectric power from coal. This could prove very important to Nova Scotia and to western Canada, where our deposits of coal are extremely important indeed. The production of cheap electric power from coal will attract industries to those areas, where industries are badly needed. We all know that industry goes to power; and if we can produce cheap power in those areas, industries

The Address-Mr. Hees will go there, because it is advantageous to them to locate in areas of that kind. Plants which are producing in central Canada at the present time will find it advantageous to put branch plants in the west and the mari-times because their cost of distribution of goods in those areas will be far less than if the goods are produced in central Canada and they have to pay the long freight haul to the maritimes and the west. If we can produce cheap by-products from coal, this will lead to the building up of important by-product industries in those areas, and they in turn will diversify the economy in those areas and make them less dependent on the primary products they produce.
We have another example of what worthwhile research can do in a large industry, in the development of new textile fabrics which would create additional sales for an industry which is hard-pressed at the present time. If, in addition to new textile fabrics, more efficient methods of production were developed, then we could lower our costs and regain our foothold in the competitive textile market.
We have here in Canada an ideal opportunity for tremendous industrial expansion which staggers the imagination. We have almost unlimited supplies of practically every raw material required in industry. We have almost unlimited sources, and potential sources, of hydroelectric power and almost every mineral one can think of, and we can produce enough food in this country to feed several times our present population. We have the capital, and we have proved we have the ability to attract more from outside, without which it would be extremely difficult to carry out large scale expansion. But even more important we have in Canada the brains which are necessary to carry out an expansion of this kind.
This expansion would be greatly aided, I believe, if we did some of the things I have mentioned. We should first of all set up a parliamentary committee to examine the possibility and best means of operating a greatly expanded research program. Second, we should reduce the high taxation which makes it very difficult to sell our products competitively in world markets. If we reduce these taxes we can thereby attract capital for new industry, bearing in mind that unless capital is attracted these new industries simply will not get started.
I would therefore urge this government to stop thinking of curing unemployment merely by making adjustments to the Unemployment Insurance Act and accelerating our public works program, necessary though those measures may be. The problem we are facing

requires far sterner measures. Unemployment is the barometer of economic progress within a country, and when it increases by anywhere from 40 to 100 per cent over the corresponding figures for last year it demonstrates that we are not nearly as healthy economically as we should be. Our exports are down; our domestic sales are dowm. Any businessman will tell you what difficult competitive conditions he has to face.
This government owes it to the country to give a lead in overcoming the basic causes of unemployment. I have suggested two measures the government could readily adopt. I sincerely hope the government will take some heed of what I have said, and give the measures I have suggested some very serious consideration. We in opposition, however, are well aware that this government finds it difficult to accept our suggestions and get moving.
In dealing with the worrying question of unemployment, I think the government should make quite certain that the money it spends in providing employment, and which it has indicated it is going to spend on increased public works, is spent wisely and productively. I believe the government would do well to study the program about to be undertaken by the government of the United States, which is a very large road-building program. I can think of no kind of public work which is more necessary in terms of expansion and development than a well conducted road-building program, because highways play a vitally important part in industrial growth.
I am not suggesting for one moment that the government should embark upon a highway building program. That, as we all know, is the function of the provinces. But the government could place a large proportion of the money it intends to spend on public works in the hands of the provinces, to enable them to undertake a large scale road-building program. Such a program would provide jobs for tomorrow as well as for today, and it would also provide constructive and profitable employment.
The government could also provide employment for many thousands of Canadians for several years ahead by making it possible for more people to buy new houses. The high rate of down payment and high interest charges have today put new houses right out of the reach of the average Canadian. If the government will reduce the down payment to a flat 10 per cent, instead of the present 15 per cent required on the cheapest N.H.A. home, it will make it possible for the average Canadian to make a down payment on a new house. The government should also

reduce the interest rate and bring it closer to the rate it pays the people of Canada for the use of their money. People might then be able to afford the carrying charges on new homes.
The suggestions I have put forward would not cost the taxpayers of this country one single cent, and their implementation would mean the provision of useful and constructive employment for thousands of Canadians. It would also enable the builders of this country to construct thousands of additional homes which are very much needed. I might add in conclusion that the construction of new highways and new homes would provide us with useful national assets for the future, and I would urge the government to give this serious consideration.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I came to Ottawa I listened to a number of throne speeches, and having listened to two in Ottawa I am struck by the fact that they have one thing in common. That is that they tend to devote a great deal of their time to telling us what we have already read in the newspapers. One might also imagine the assumption was that members of parliament not merely look but actually are illiterate.
For instance, we were told that we were hosts here in Ottawa to the Colombo plan consultative committee. Most of us, I think, were already well aware of that fact. But I was interested in noting that the government did not have the temerity to put in His Excellency's mouth the information that we were going to increase our grant by the magnificent sum of $1 million. Possibly the luncheon cheque for the consultative committee that the government presumably picked up was too high to allow us to do anything more generous than increase it by $1 million.
Of course, we hear rumours as to why our contribution to that plan is being held within such strict limits. A very well known Canadian editor suggested a few weeks ago that there were elements within the Liberal cabinet which were anxious to deal perhaps more practically and generously with this problem of the development of Asia than certain other members of the cabinet. In fact, it was suggested in that broadcast that a certain well known avuncular figure in this country was actually the Mr. Scrooge who prevented Canada from contributing more generously.
When I heard that broadcast I was reminded of the fact that we in Canada have had a considerable amount of debunking of legendary figures. We had Dr. Brock Chisholm,
The Address-Mr. C. Cameron of course, who got into trouble in debunking Santa Claus. Now we have editors and parliamentary critics pulling the whiskers aside from Santa Claus and showing behind them a much sterner and less benevolent figure than is usually presented to the public of Canada. All in all, if this goes on Canada is going to be in a bad way for fairy tales. We shall have no avuncular figure, no Santa Claus; we shall have just hard, cold, cruel facts in a hard, cold, cruel political world.
Before the throne speech was finished, after going half-way through telling us what we already knew, it began to embark on mild prophecies for the future. It starts first of all with the government's projected increase in the war veterans allowance. I suppose everyone in this chamber was greatly relieved to hear that. But do you remember, Mr. Speaker, the number of speeches made in this chamber urging this very same government-and it is the same government, except for a few defections in the meantime-to implement some improvements to the War Veterans Allowance Act, and how we were told it could not be done? I wonder whether our new Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) would care to stand up in the house and tell us that we can afford it this year but we could not afford it last year? Or is the explanation perhaps a rather grimmer one? Is it that the problem of war veterans year by year becomes a less expensive financial proposition for the Canadian people to carry? If that is the case, all I can say is that the government should be consistent and go on refusing, and the problem will solve itself.
Again, of course, one heard last year that the same restraining force operated in the cabinet to prevent that generous action which is now being taken. It may or it may not be true. However, we know that many of those who would have benefited last year if this government had taken this action will not be with us this year to benefit from it. That is something I think every member of the Liberal party should search his conscience about. Every member of the Liberal party should bear in mind the fact that there were many veterans who would have benefited last year but who are now no longer with us to take advantage of this proposal.
We have another prophecy of action on the part of our government in the future, which action we have already taken in this chamber. That is, of course, the improvement to the Unemployment Insurance Act, if indeed "improvement" is the word we should use. There has been a slight relaxation of the terms of that act in order to deal, over a short period, with the problems it is meant to cope with.

The Address

Mr. C. Cameron Again we have a strange spectacle, Mr. Speaker. I also remember the number of speeches that were made last year in this chamber urging this self-same government to take this action at that time. One can only conclude that the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Maclnnis) was correct the other day when he suggested that the reason the government has now decided that something must be done is that there are more voices raised in protest this year than there were last year; and of course the more voices that are raised in protest, the more political danger there is for our government. So again we have a question of the government being pushed after delaying for one year, and offering no logical explanation now for dealing with this problem that was also with us last year.
When I see the way in which they deal with the unemployment problem I am rather reminded of the old gag they used to have about the Russians who were being pursued. This was in the days before the bolsheviks, in the days of the grand dukes and the troikas. You remember they were being pursued by wolves and the watchword was "throw out another baby". Of course, eventually they came to the end of the babies and the wolves were snapping at their heels. In spite of all the mild palliatives in the Unemployment Insurance Act, I suggest that the wolves of economic depression will still be snapping at our heels next year or in fact before next year rolls around.
During the course of this debate one suggestion was made which interested me greatly. That was the Suggestion by the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) to the effect that we should depart from the policy pursued by this government in this matter of housing and protect not only the lending institutions but those who make down payments on buildings under the National Housing Act. I am glad to offer my voice in support of that suggestion, although I would remind the house, and those who were members of the banking and commerce committee last year, that we raised the question in the committee last year but neither the hon. member for Spadina nor any of his Liberal colleagues thought that it was a good idea at that time. I can see no particular technical difficulties involved in ensuring that the person who purchases a house under the National Housing Act shall be assured of retaining his equity or at least his equity minus some possible deductions for rental for any term of occupancy he may have had with regard to the premises. Personally I think that can be done. But, as with all the other measures this government introduces


for the benefit of the people of Canada, I suppose we shall have to wait at least twelve months before they get around to doing it.
So much for what is in the throne speech. I want to spend a few moments before I sit down on a matter that I think perhaps is of more fundamental importance to us than even these serious questions of unemployment, the plight of the war veterans and the problem of housing in Canada. Some while ago I noticed an article in a periodical for which I have not a particularly high regard, but the article was of such striking importance that I did some investigation on it in order to fmd out whether or not it was merely, shall we say, some loose talking by Time magazine.
Some hon. members have probably read the article to which I refer. It appeared last month. It was a rather disturbing article describing a paper that was read before the French Academy of Sciences by a young physicist by the name of Charles Noel Martin, sponsored by a man who is probably the leading physicist in Europe and a Nobel prize winner, namely Prince Louis de Broglie. In this paper this young man charged that there was a conspiracy of silence throughout the world as to the possible and probable results of continued experimentation with H-bombs in the world. He suggested that there were a number of extremely dangerous possibilities.
The first one he listed was the danger of permanent and deleterious effects on our climate. When I read that suggestion I remembered that just before I left England in November of last year Professor Frederick Soddy, another Nobel prize winner, had a letter in the London Times, in which he denounced as irresponsible those scientists who were claiming that there was no possible connection between our rather deplorable climatic conditions that have obtained over the last twelve months or so and these heavy thermonuclear explosions in different parts of the world. Professor Soddy pointed out that by means of those explosions we are doing on a gigantic scale the sort of thing that so-called rainmakers do on a small scale with their limited facilities.
This young man who presented the paper to the French Academy of Sciences pointed out that in the last two years there have been approximately ten hydrogen bombs exploded in different parts of the world, each of which is equal to from 1,000 to 2,500 times the strength of the A-bomb dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The most important danger foreseen by this young man, supported by Prince Louis de Broglie and other scientific experts, has been the danger of long-continuing or in fact permanent damage to the genetic inheritance of human beings.

Today, right here in the city of Ottawa, I was talking to a young man who is a survivor of the bombing of Hiroshima. This young man tells me that even now, ten years after the bombing, he has to report once a week for a medical check-up and a blood count. When I was speaking to him today he told me of the number of people who have died many years after that explosion, of children who were born, in some cases some years after the explosion, who have not lived to survive, perhaps mercifully, because they probably would have survived as extremely defective human beings.
I received from the Japanese embassy a document that has just been produced by the atomic bomb injuries investigating committee on the case history of one of the Japanese fishermen who was dusted, as they call it, with atomic fall-out from the Bikini trials of March 1 of last year. This man, Aikichi Kuboyama, died in September, and this document says in part:
A series of announcements have been made from time to time by the authorities concerned regarding the incident and the unfortunate victims. Kubo-yama's death, however, gave rise to a wave of charges and counter-charges, of rumours and speculations, over the treatment of the affected fishermen and the probable cause of the Kuboyama demise.
There is need to clear the air of misunderstanding, and a summary of the medical facts known to date of the twenty-three victims should serve that end.
Here is what they found when they examined them, and these were examinations conducted by both Japanese and American medical men. They found that the disease was acute radiation sickness, that such external injuries as depilation-hairlessness-* dermatitis, skin ulcers, pustules, blisters and necrosis were noticeable on the head and the upper part of the bodies of all patients at the time they were hospitalized.
I see some hon. members smiling over this. To me it is quite shocking that anyone can consider these appalling dangers as in any way amusing. As a matter of fact there is no one in this chamber with the knowledge to deny the actuality of these dangers. Yet throughout the world people are turning a deaf ear to those who can tell us of the grave dangers of permanent genetic damage to the human race. That to my mind, Mr. Speaker, is the ultimate blasphemy.
Men have destroyed themselves and each other with varying degrees of cruelty all through recorded history, but it has been left for this age and this generation to destroy generations yet unborn, to condemn them to being born defective physically, mentally, or both. These are real dangers, so those who know tell us.
The Address-Mr. C. Cameron
I would not have brought up this matter if I had not had some idea of a practical suggestion for dealing with the question. I am not going to suggest anything so naive as begging the three culprit nations to desist. The United States, the Soviet union and Great Britain can only be described as culprit nations who are persisting in these unnecessary and dangerous experiments. I am, however, taking a leaf out of the book of Bertrand, Lord Russell, the famous scientist and philosopher of Great Britain, who not long ago, you may remember, wrote an article in which he suggested a method by which the final descent into atomic war might be prevented. He suggested the appointment of a committee of scientists to draw up an objective statement of the results of atomic war.
I wish the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) were here, because I think perhaps one should occasionally wound his feelings as we did last year. I am suggesting that here is something Canada can do to retrieve Canada's rather inglorious record in international affairs in the last ten years. Here is something practical our delegates to the United Nations can do. They can move for the setting up of a committee of competent scientists, physicists, biologists, psychologists and medical men to give us a report on the probable, possible and certain results of the continued explosion of hydrogen bombs in the world.
It may be objected that we cannot find out exactly what strength of bomb has been used or is going to be used. I do not believe that for one moment. I have not the slightest doubt that every person in the world who is competent to understand-and it is a very small number of people-is fully aware of the magnitude of the explosions that have taken place in the Soviet union, in Australia and in the south Pacific. They know, at least within near enough limits, what forces they have to examine the results. I would suggest that if our delegates at the United Nations would call for the appointment of suich a committee, and if such a committee were to present its report to the world, then no government would dare to continue with these experiments,, which are unnecessary from the point of view of proving the efficacy of this devilish weapon whose dangers, according to those people who know, may very well result in the complete degeneration of the human species.
I think if our delegates at the United Nations were to do that it might well be that Canada's place in the niche of history would be a more resplendent one than it has been to date or will be by burying our

The Address-Mr. Hanna heads in the sand and pretending that these dangers do not exist. I offer that as a very serious suggestion to our government before the next meeting of the United Nations in New York.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like other members who have spoken before me I too should like to offer congratulations to the mover (Mr. Leduc) and the seconder (Mr. Carrick) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne for the very fine job they have done.
At the outset I should like to make a brief reference to some events connected with the province, and particularly the city, from which I come and which I have the honour to represent. During the past year both the province of Alberta and the city of Edmonton have continued to grow and develop at a steadily accelerating pace. In every branch of that growth and development that I can think of new records have been set. The population is still growing in both Edmonton and Alberta generally, and industrialization is increasing very rapidly and along the soundest possible lines.
This gives us a growing sense of pride in our city and our province, not only because we like our community to grow and prosper but more especially because of the effect these conditions are bound to have on the economy of the whole Canadian nation. A strong and growing Edmonton and a strong and growing Alberta make for a strong and growing Canada.
These conditions of progress which we are experiencing in full measure in Alberta are, fortunately fqr all of us, fairly general throughout the whole of Canada. Small wonder then that we Canadians sing with justifiable and ever-increasing pride:
With glowing hearts we see thee rise,
The true north, strong and free.
Last fall Edmonton celebrated its golden jubilee as a city. The occasion was marked by a pageant, which gave a stirring review of the events of the past fifty years and the role of the many pioneers who have carried the city of Edmonton forward to her present greatness. To further accentuate the keynote of progress, work has commenced on the erection of a new city hall which will be a structure appropriate to the greatness of the city. I was glad that on the occasion of the dedication of the site for the new city hall two federal ministers of the crown were present, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) and the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham), together with provincial and civic representatives. The presence of two federal cabinet ministers there on that occasion helped to

emphasize what I have in mind, namely that progress in any or all the different parts of Canada is an enhancement of the nation as a whole.
During the present year the province of Alberta will celebrate its golden jubilee, and once again the occasion will be suitably observed. Her sister province of Saskatchewan, another gem in the illustrious array of the ten provinces of Canada, will likewise celebrate its fiftieth anniversary. Both these provinces were brought into being by the federal Liberal government in 1905, and both have achieved remarkable progress in the past 50 years. It can, I believe, be truly said of the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, as it was said of the original fathers of confederation:	Divine Providence being their
guide, they builded better than they knew.
While there is not time for me to mention, much less to enlarge upon, all the particular items which have contributed to Alberta's prosperity, I think it is only right for me to say that the greatest of these developments has been the vast petrochemical industry, which is located in the federal riding of Edmonton-Strathcona.
I believe I would be pardoned if I made reference to the well known fact that Edmonton is now the home of the famous and much sought 'after Grey cup. Other hon. members, particularly those from the east, may be interested in learning that all possible precautions are being taken to keep it there. Personally I can think of no finer setting for such an outstanding trophy of sport. We won it in 1954 to celebrate Edmonton's golden jubilee and we hope to win it again in 1955 to celebrate Alberta's golden jubilee.
Another outstanding event scheduled for 1955 is the completion of arrangements to bring Alberta natural gas to the cities of eastern Canada, as well as to the west coast. Both east and west already are enjoying the benefits of Alberta oil. We are glad that both will soon enjoy the incomparable service of Alberta natural gas.
And so, Mr. Speaker, the Grey cup moves west and Alberta oil and gas go east. What more tangible evidence could there be of our growing national strength in all parts of the country? What better demonstration could we have of our ever-growing national unity? This is the sort of thing which adds immensely to the strengthening of our national ties, which all true Canadians so ardently desire.
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne gives promise of many things that are dear

to the hearts of Canadians. It makes reference to peace, progress and humanity, all of which the government will endeavour to promote further during this session of parliament. I was particularly gratified to hear that measures are being taken to relieve the necessitous circumstances in which many of our older veterans and widows of veterans find themselves. Veterans' organizations, such as the Canadian Legion, are to be commended for keeping the plight of these people to the fore, and the government is to be congratulated on its recognition that there is need for some improvement in their situation. I am sure all hon. members will look forward with keen interest to the detailed proposals, which will be brought forward later on in the matter of the war veterans allowance.
Likewise the government is to be very highly commended for its proposed amendments to the Blind Persons Act. The amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act which we have just passed are most timely. Various measures placed on the statute books by this government for the relief of need and suffering are models of humanitarianism, and as such are strongly supported by the majority of Canadians.
Along humanitarian lines, too, is the proposal to increase aid under the Colombo plan. I find Canadians everywhere full of enthusiasm for this splendid program which our government helped bring into existence. To lend a helping hand to those in need is always worth while. To show less fortunate peoples a better way than communism is, I am sure, in our best interests as well as theirs.
I believe that all hon. members, especially those who have had some direct association with municipal affairs, will welcome the proposals to re-examine the Municipal Grants Act. Our growing development, and indeed prosperity, in Canada have produced some very acute problems for our municipal governments. Because our municipalities render services to federal government property, I have long felt that they are in justice entitled to adequate payment for those services.
Grants in lieu of full taxation on federal property would be a blessing to many municipalities which are heavily burdened with the rising costs of education. I realize that constitutionally education is a provincial problem, but I am most anxious that the federal government make some contribution to help the hard pressed municipalities of this country. I believe the real soluton to the problems of all three levels of government is to place all three of them in a
The Address-Mr. Hanna financial position to discharge their responsibilities. Unfortunately for our municipal governments they seem to be the ones in the most difficult position financially, and they are least able of the three to correct the situation.
Likewise, those Canadians responsible for our municipal government will be relieved to learn of the proposal to increase the grade crossing fund. The slowing up of our commerce because of grade crossings, and the rising toll of accidents at them, gives this problem a top priority. As Canada grows the grade crossing problem also grows. I am confident that this house will act swiftly to translate proposals along this line into action. More separated grade crossings will not only reduce accidents but will give employment as well. I will admit frankly that we need more separated grade crossings at Edmonton, and we need them immediately.
As an Albertan I would like to say that we rejoice in the steps that have been taken to make the St. Lawrence seaway a reality. It may, we hope, help us with our freight rate problem, which we in the west feel very keenly. But apart from that we are convinced that this great project is in the best interests of the Canadian nation as a whole, and what helps Canada forward will surely and inevitably help Alberta, just as truly as what helps Alberta also helps Canada. Being good Canadians, Albertans encourage and support any measure that helps build a greater and a better Canada.
I would like to digress for a moment to express appreciation to two departments of the government that have recently made announcements of particular interest to my constituency. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) has recently announced, in conjunction with the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham), a decision that will give Edmonton a new major civilian airport. Some hon. members may be surprised to hear this, since the existing Edmonton airport has become justly famous both far and wide. But things happen fast in Edmonton these days. And so it is that just as surely as we have lived up to our slogan, "Aerial Crossroads of the World", inevitably, the increasing air traffic has outgrown the crossroads. In order to maintain her role in the national economy Edmonton's famous airport finds it necessary to move to a new and larger site, just as many prosperous businesses are doing all over the country. Air transport is developing so rapidly that I respectfully urge the minister to take all possible measures to arrange for the new location as soon as possible. I urge this matter not only in the interests of the city but in the national interest as well.



The Address-Mr. Hanna
The other minister whom I would like to compliment is the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters), who recently announced that the thriving town of Fort Saskatchewan is to have a proper post office. The thousands of people whom this new post office will serve will be most grateful for this development.
This evening we have all enjoyed, because some hon. members gave evidence of it, the exposition of the Social Credit technique by the financial spokesman for the Social Credit party. I think we can take it that the views expressed by the hon. member for Lethbridge represent the official views of the Social Credit party, since I have never heard any of their members deny those particular views that were outlined this evening. I wonder how the party leader, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), reconciles the views we heard this evening with his statement the other day that his party is the real free enterprise party. How can he reconcile a government-dictated price structure with free enterprise? I should like to hear him deal with that subject. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that he can only have a government-dictated price system under a dictatorship.

This government, under the inspiring leadership of our great Prime Minister, is solidly based in the hearts and minds of the Canadian people. Mr. Speaker, with no further ado, I wish to state my opinion on this long, interminable piece de resistance which Her Majesty's representative was forced to read to us and which is called the speech from the throne. On close and repeated examination it reveals itself as what it really is, that is to say, a flood of words in a desert of ideas, and nothing else.
A group of men who believe themselves to be serious, who make up the Canadian cabinet and upon whom devolves the responsibility for drafting this speech have nothing to offer but this endless avalanche of words containing no new ideas except

those borrowed from representations and suggestions put forward by Progressive Conservative members in the course of previous sessions. Looking directly at the Liberal members across the way I do feel moved to exclaim: All's quiet on the horizon!
Mr. Speaker, I have had the opportunity of making a very modest but sincere contribution to the debate at the resolution stage of legislation designed to extend the period for payment of insurance benefits to those who have a legal right to receive such benefits. I said then, and I repeat it now, that those workers who have had to suffer, over the years, from the running sore of unemployment-not regional nor seasonal, but permanent

are not satisfied with the application of this innocuous poultice to a gaping wound.

I am of course speaking of unemployment and I must say that, in view of its disquieting spread, the application of a poultice has now become insufficient. The government is ill-advised to bring but slight relief.
In order to create a feeling of satisfaction, which will only be temporary, in order to give hope to those who, with their family, experience great hardships at this time because of unemployment, the speech from the throne proposes that an increased subsidy be voted to the departments concerned for use in more elaborate public works.
What will be the nature of these works? No one knows and the speech from the throne casts no light on the matter. Aware of the constant policy of inaction of the Liberal party, I believe I am not mistaken in stating that these works will consist, as always, in contracts being awarded to certain contractors.
There is nothing in all that, Mr. Speaker, to remedy the alarming conditions which must face the workers who are presently living a life of anxiety that one can easily imagine.
This Liberal government is the one responsible for the economic depression we are now going through and it must not shirk the responsibility which rests upon it to check

that depression as soon as possible. Now more than ever is the time to give up its policy of inaction which traditionally has been that of the Liberal party and to replace it with a policy fitted to the urgent needs of the day, or to leave the economic recovery of our country to those who are better disposed to remedy such ills.
The public works program must be national in scope since we find that unemployment is at the epidemic stage all over the country. As far as my county and the city of Quebec are concerned, the needs have been obvious for a number of years and the Liberal politicians have always failed to resort to the solution which had been requested earnestly and very often by every important public body in the old capital city.
To my mind-and I am voicing here the general opinion of the people of Quebec-the deepening of the St. Charles river, the works to prevent the pollution of the Lairet river, and the removing of railway crossings are the only projects which could bring relief to those who seek work.
However, I warn the government against political discrimination which, much too often, comes into the picture when those works are undertaken. All allegiances must be put aside in order to give employment to those who have an absolute need of it. I never heard it said that distress and hunger had a particular political colour.
I take the liberty of submitting to the house that at Christmastime, all public men in my county, putting aside political affiliations, acted together in order to provide many needy families with the food they required to spend a cheerful Christmas. Our only concern then was to feed those who were really in need. Such an example should inspire in the future those who sit on the other side.
It is very interesting to note the amount the government will spend for the unemployed in the form of public works. Will that amount be sufficient to deal satisfactorily with the problem or so insignificant that only a few will be prevented from dying of hunger?
I am expecting the answer that will be forthcoming from the government after a while, that they were unable to do better, because the appropriations did not allow for such a large expenditure.
I dare hope that the colossal joke of 1939 will not be repeated in 1955; nobody would take it seriously anyway.
I cannot forget this absurd answer made by the late Mackenzie King, then Liberal prime minister of Canada, to the then gov-50433- I5i

The authorities of the government of Quebec got a definite no, as an answer, and the prime minister added:	"We have no
money".
However, hardly two months later, Canada hastened to declare war on Germany. And what happened then? The federal government opened wide the treasury and millions and billions of dollars were spent with that well known prodigality. We were told that we had to set up a powerful army that would fight on the battlefields of Europe in the defence of Christianity and civilization. Mr. Speaker, civilization was already threatened at home. Our people had been going hungry for a long time through lack of employment. Civilization had lost its true meaning because in a country like ours, possessing unlimited resources, a terrible depression had fallen upon us in the manner of plagues and calamities.
Government-controlled war plants mushroomed and munition manufacturers rejoiced at the thought of making enormous sums of money at the expense of our sons' blood.
Our lavishness went as far as making loans of billions of dollars to other countries, without interest, while the debtor nations lost no time in lending that money to other faraway countries, but with interest.
You must have noted, Mr. Speaker, that two months previously, a few millions could not be found to undertake, in Quebec, public works which would have taken us out of the misery in which the poor administration of the government had thrown thousands of families. The working people of Quebec were not then asking for charity, through the government of their province, any more than they are begging for it now; all they wanted was to earn the income necessary and essential to provide for themselves and their families.
We did not have a few million dollars for living works, but we were throwing away countless billions to propagate death. Nevertheless I must state unequivocally, though regretfully, that the only times during which our people have known any kind of prosperity, even of the most fictitious sort, were those during which nations were at each other's throats and Canada was sacrificing on the battlefields a part, the best part I should say, of that youth upon which we had laid our fondest hopes for the future.

The Address-Mr. Dufresne
That is a nonsensical situation. It is our duty to put an end to this as soon as possible. Consciously or not we are rushing headlong into tragedy, or else we are quickly moving towards a damnable ideology which on the other hand we would be prepared, possibly, to fight at the cost of heavy sacrifice. Since the government seem to believe that unemployment is entirely within their jurisdiction, I will say to them, with that frankness which is a characteristic of mine: "All right, mind your own business, but do mind it seriously!"
The speech from the throne announces that amendments will be made to the War Veterans Allowance Act in order to raise the basic rates as well as the ceiling on permissible incomes of recipients of allowances. It has finally dawned upon the government, Mr. Speaker, that it was time to improve the fate of those who, having left behind country, home, folks and friends, besides risking then-lives for the protection of Canada, came back crippled in one way or another or in failing health. This government cannot claim credit for this increase, for I know that the war veterans will prove their gratitude to the Progressive Conservative party. If at last they are given a recognition which will never equal the sacrifices they have made, they will owe it to all of those who, on this side of the house, have never ceased to plead in their behalf.
I should also like to speak on behalf of the veterans of the first world war who today, having reached a certain age, deserve as much consideration, since they made the same sacrifices in 1914-18. I therefore hope that they will not be forgotten.
It might be in order to remind the minister concerned that the humane thing to do would be to order that these veterans of the 191418 war, whose pension is insufficient, or those who get no pension at all, be employed in the corps of commissionaires or at any other such work. I would be the first to congratulate him for such a move if he were to agree to my suggestion.
